title: How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Moment of Reckoning
content: In early 2023, Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman gathered with Jas Khaira, the company’s lead AI investor, and other top executives at the finance giant’s Park Avenue headquarters in Manhattan for a debate: Should they give billions of dollars to a little-known data center developer—CoreWeave—that they had turned down just a few months earlier? CoreWeave had gotten Blackstone to return to the table after landing a multiyear, multibillion-dollar contract to sell cloud computing services to Microsoft. It needed $2.3 billion to buy Nvidia GPUs and secure a data center to house them. In Blackstone’s discussion of the deal, several executives in the room had deep misgivings, according to a person who attended the meeting. CoreWeave was still something of a mystery, a six-year-old, privately held firm that had generated only $16 million in revenue in the previous year. Schwarzman himself was personally worried his investment team could be making a mistake, the person said. Still, Schwarzman signed off, and Blackstone went ahead with the deal anyway. Its confidence in making the loan was rooted in the fact that the debt was structured largely on Microsoft’s ability to keep paying CoreWeave. Besides, Blackstone was eager to get in on the action of the AI boom. These days, CoreWeave is a publicly traded outfit worth $35 billion, holding cloud computing contracts with Microsoft, Meta Platforms, OpenAI and other customers that added up to $5.1 billion in revenue last year. But lately, many people have been asking themselves the same question the Blackstone suits pondered—whether investing in CoreWeave was actually a big fat mistake. With a business built on mounds of debt, CoreWeave stands today at a moment of reckoning that is reigniting concerns about the stability of the AI economy. Investors in the company have been heading for the exits. Those fears have seeped into other stocks, too, and have prompted anxious discussions across Silicon Valley and Wall Street about whether October 2026 could possibly end up resembling March 2000—the moment when the dot-com bubble burst. In the last week, the company’s stock has sharply declined—from nearly $80 a share last Tuesday to just over $61 on Monday—a roughly 20% drop that far outpaced the broader market’s decline of less than 1%. CoreWeave belongs to a group of young companies called neoclouds that offer cloud computing services competing with those of Amazon, Google and Microsoft. Shares of Nebius and IREN, two other publicly traded neoclouds, have respectively lost 15% and 17% in a week. CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator acknowledged the whipsaw in a staff memo last week. “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally,” he wrote. “We are confident in our disciplined execution.” The plunge in CoreWeave shares seems to come from an array of factors. There wasn’t any single disastrous announcement by CoreWeave in the last few days that shook confidence. But benchmark U.S. bond yields have been increasing, which means CoreWeave will almost certainly need to pay more for the financing it needs to keep growing. And last Wednesday, the latest U.S. inflation data showed a spike in prices in September, increasing the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates, which would further increase borrowing costs. At the same time, the yields on CoreWeave’s existing debt have spiked, climbing to more than 15% last week, a signal that investors were growing increasingly nervous about the company’s ability to repay its debts. Meanwhile, its CEO has sold CoreWeave stock every week between April and the end of September, securities filings show, while his fellow co-founders have also been selling regularly. While those sales were prescheduled, investors often see such transactions as signals that they, too, should sell. Trying to decipher what’s going on with CoreWeave—and what will happen next—has become a favorite water-cooler topic in Silicon Valley. Last week, for instance, Elon Musk retweeted a chart showing CoreWeave’s rising bond yields with a single word: “Yikes.” And when venture capitalist Ben Horowitz made a Thursday appearance on the “All-In” podcast, he described CoreWeave’s business as a “Rube Goldberg financial machine” and said his firm, Andreessen Horowitz, has largely stayed away from investing in companies like CoreWeave because of their debt-heavy strategies. (Andreessen Horowitz does own a stake in Volta, a newly created neocloud formed by former Brookfield infrastructure investors.) When asked to comment for this story, CoreWeave declined to make any executives available for interviews. Instead, a spokesperson sent a three-page document titled “Financing Overview October 2026” that outlined its debt maneuvers and how it plans to repay its obligations. The document ends with an attempt at succinct optimism: “CoreWeave is well-positioned to help shape [its] market as it grows and evolves.” With cloud computing and data centers at the heart of the AI era, CoreWeave’s ability to keep going is seen as an important bellwether for the entire AI industry, an outsize position for a firm that remains little known—and little understood—beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley insiders. Worries about whether CoreWeave may stumble amid rising borrowing costs then lead to broader concerns about what dominoes may fall next. Other storm clouds have gathered over the landscape. Last weekend, Microsoft said it would pull out of a compute deal with London-based Nscale over power issues that threaten to delay a 50-megawatt data center in rural Britain. And a week earlier, Firmus, an Australian data center operator backed by Nvidia and Blackstone, pulled its IPO. A day before Firmus yanked its public offering, one CoreWeave executive, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the company had not authorized him to speak publicly, argued that CoreWeave investors shouldn’t see that as a warning sign for CoreWeave. He sought to differentiate CoreWeave from Firmus by highlighting the former’s deeper stockpile of long-term contracts, which he says isn’t the same for Firmus. “They have some contracts—and some potential,” the executive said. Jerry Tang, CEO of AIB Data Centers, a small data center developer, has been biting his nails while watching CoreWeave’s declining stock price. “This is a classic liquidity crunch,” said Tang, whose firm just signed a contract with Nebius to provide 50 MW of data center capacity. “I am very concerned, because this affects everybody,” including his new partner, he added. Short of Compute CoreWeave got its start when a group of hedge fund commodities traders decided to get into crypto mining. They set up in a New Jersey office in 2017, starting with one and later expanding to many Nvidia GPUs, which are essential for running the computations involved in crypto mining. A crash in cryptocurrency prices the following year convinced them to use their pile of chips for something else. They pivoted toward high-performance cloud computing, renaming their company from Atlantic Crypto to CoreWeave along the way. As CoreWeave turned its attention to the cloud, it saw debt as a way to supercharge its growth. Then as now, one form of debt it favored allowed it to raise money for specific data center projects anchored by large customers—like Microsoft. Following ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch, Microsoft quickly found itself short of compute after promising OpenAI that it would provide the computing power for the company’s nascent models. In February 2023, CoreWeave signed its compute deal with Microsoft. Two months later, Nvidia joined a $221 million round of financing for CoreWeave, throwing its support behind a competitor to the traditional cloud giants—Amazon, Google and Microsoft—as part of a bid to diversify its reliance on the firms that buy its chips. By the time CoreWeave got the loan from Blackstone in August of that year, the two firms had come up with an innovative financial maneuver, backing the $2.3 billion with AI chips as collateral. That provided a template for CoreWeave’s future borrowing. For each data center project, CoreWeave secures a contract with a customer. It then uses that agreement to line up financing, structuring the loans to pay down the debt with the revenue earned from the contract. The company has said it should take two and a half years to repay such a loan as it continues collecting payouts through the entire life of the contract. In a staff memo last week, CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator acknowledged his company’s gyrating stock price:  “When you are building a new type of technology company, there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” (Getty Images) To fund its operations, CoreWeave borrows additional debt that isn’t tied to its contracts and must be repaid out of the corporate coffers. It uses some of those funds, according to analysts, to pay for costs that aren’t covered by the project loans. That means the company is piling debt on top of debt. Armed with Blackstone’s money, CoreWeave continued working closely with Microsoft, adding other customers like Meta Platforms and OpenAI along the way. In March 2025, CoreWeave sold shares to the public at $40 a share, then the largest AI-related listing ever. The stock surged beyond $183 in the months after. In July, CoreWeave became the first company to deploy Nvidia’s most advanced server rack, and this January, the chipmaker invested another $2 billion in the company. As CoreWeave grew, it continued using the loan structure it designed with Blackstone to fund its expansion. As one of the few companies that actually trades in the public markets, CoreWeave has also become a proxy for the broader AI trade. Many investors who have long exposure to private tech companies such as the leading frontier labs have turned to CoreWeave as a way to hedge other investments, according to one adviser who speaks with numerous large investors. To hedge, they can short the stock. They can also buy credit default swaps, which offer a payout if the company defaults on its debt. “If you are taking a negative bet, what better place than in a liquid bet on [credit default swaps] for CoreWeave?” said John McPeake, an analyst at Rosenblatt Securities, who rates the stock a buy. McPeake said he attended CoreWeave’s customer conference several weeks ago in San Francisco, where the company said it would raise prices an additional 10%, on top of an increase it had already announced, on the main product it sells: GPUs by the hour. ‘We Can’t Figure It Out’ Despite all the recent commotion, CoreWeave still enjoys the support of the industry’s biggest players. In addition to having connections to Blackstone, the private equity firm with the most assets under management, the company also enjoys cozy ties to Nvidia. Last Thursday, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had full confidence in CoreWeave. “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” he said. “I’m optimistic.” The comments arrested the slide in the company’s stock price before it picked up again on Friday. And early backer Blackstone has more recently introduced the company to a new base of investors: insurance companies. CoreWeave finds insurers alluring because they have deep pockets and generally invest with long-term time horizons. Brannin McBee, a CoreWeave founder, acknowledged the importance of the insurance segment last week in an FT interview published just as the company’s bonds were plunging . Steve Schwarzman’s Blackstone has been a major partner for CoreWeave, most recently helping it win insurance giants as investors in its debt offerings. (Getty Images) Insurance companies, which like to invest in high-yielding investment-grade debt, bought more than $740 million of a project-specific loan CoreWeave had arranged for a Meta contract, according to data compiled by S&P Capital IQ. Blackstone manages investments for some of the largest insurers involved in the deal, including American General Life Insurance, Fidelity & Guaranty Life and Security Life of Denver. The next thing on the horizon for CoreWeave could be equity sales. Michael Haber, a desk credit strategist at Jefferies, said last week in an interview that he has had a lot of conversations with equity investors who have finally taken notice that higher interest rates and too much supply of AI-related debt are making the credit markets more expensive—and perhaps totally unavailable in the future—for some data center projects and chip purchases. They’re coming to the realization that neoclouds and other developers are going to need to raise money by selling stock. “A lot of equity investors were not paying attention and are now waking up and saying, ‘Why is the equity down so much?’” he said. “The AI story is moving from being a tech story to a financing story.” Selling that story to investors could be difficult if stock and bond prices continue to fluctuate without a clear reason why. Last week, even CoreWeave’s bankers at Goldman Sachs couldn’t explain the swoon in the company’s share price. When Christopher Miglino, CEO of compute provider Axe Compute, sat down with his bankers at Goldman Sachs, they acknowledged that there was no fundamental reason why CoreWeave should have been hammered so hard. Goldman was one of the company’s IPO underwriters. “I was having breakfast with Goldman Sachs yesterday, and I said, ‘What do you guys think?’” Miglino said. “They said, ‘We can’t figure it out. Fundamentally, there is no rhyme and reason for what’s going on.’” On Monday, Goldman’s research analysts upgraded CoreWeave’s stock to a buy rating. Such moves can often bring some relief to a battered stock. Even so, CoreWeave shares finished the day down 0.4%.

title: Interpretability Is the Key to Physical AI, Says World Mechanics CEO Sonia Joseph
content: Two of the hardest problems in AI right now are creating models that understand the physical world—so called world models —and making sense of the internal workings of AI models—otherwise known as mechanistic interpretability . Typically, these are treated as two separate problems: researchers working on world models are often not concerned with their internal workings, and interpretability researchers tend to focus on the language models that power most AI tools we currently use. But Sonia Joseph, the co-founder and CEO of a new startup, World Mechanics, argues that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin . Joseph joined the latest episode of AI Deep Dive to explain that connection, which could be key to making AI useful in the physical world, from medicine to manufacturing. ( The full episode is available here .) “You need interpretability to have world models,” she said. “You need to be looking at their internal representations. You need to be using that to guide training for data efficiency, for performance, and also for reliability, and physical safety and security.” For example, if an AI model is guiding a surgeon through an operation, “how do I know that’s not a hallucination?” Joseph asked. Identifying the concepts that AI model has learned could help ensure that the AI is not basing its decision on “spurious cues, like the color of the surgeon’s mask, or does the surgeon have a ring on their finger, which current world models do.” We also discussed why Joseph does not think that language models automating AI research will work for the physical world, the ways in which she disagrees with her former colleague Yann LeCun, and how AI systems could be interpretable to blue collar workers rather than exclusively to academics. The following transcript of the conversation has been lightly edited for clarity. Drew: Welcome back to the Information’s AI Deep Dive. On this show, we get to the bottom of the hardest technical problems in AI. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. My guest today is Sonia Joseph. Sonia is the co-founder and CEO of World Mechanics, a startup that’s working on training interpretable world models. Meaning, we want the physical world to be understood by our AIs, and we also want those AIs to be understood by us. Before co-founding World Mechanics, Sonia was a researcher at Meta, where she led Meta’s forum on interpretability. Thanks for coming on the show, Sonia. Joseph: Thank you so much, Rocket. I’m so excited to be here. Drew: Me too. I’m really glad you’re here. I think we probably first met maybe three years ago or so at a dinner that Neel Nanda, an interpretability researcher at DeepMind, hosted, and it was over at a Nepalese restaurant in Berkeley. And this comes to mind because I think every time we talk, I start craving Nepalese food. Joseph: It’s a great association. I still think about the food. Drew: I’m totally conditioned. Yeah, it was a great conversation. But now I think I’m gonna have to get dumplings after this. Joseph: Oh, okay. You’re making me hungry now. Drew: I’m excited. Joseph: Me too. That’s great. Drew: Well, I’m really glad you’re on the show today, we’re going to talk about this intersection between interpretability and world models, which are two—I mean—fascinating topics in their own right. But we’re going to get into the intersection between them. I want to start with a post that you wrote, claiming that world models and interpretability are two sides of the same coin. I think that’s kind of a provocative claim. I guess usually when I hear people talk about the importance of interpreting models, they’re talking about language models, talking about chatbots and language-based agents. And then when people talk about world models, they’re sort of talking about a whole nother universe. They’re talking about models that understand the physical world for manufacturing or for robotics. But often these two things are not in conversation with each other. So, can you explain why these are two sides of the same coin? Joseph: Okay, so world model has become a very slippery term, and there is an East Coast definition of world models that’s often used in New York and Montreal, where I was for the last five years. And then there’s a West Coast definition, which listeners here and people here are probably more familiar with. So, I’d say interpretability is baked into the East Coast definition. In the East Coast, which is full of neuroscientists, there’s also a lot of thought about internal representation. So, what is the neural net representing, and does it map one to one with the physical world? So this can be a proxy for true physical reasoning or physical understanding. And I sometimes use the term physical reasoning instead of world model to prevent confusion from the West Coast definition. And the West Coast definition often focuses on either one of two aspects. One is either generating very photorealistic worlds. This is a hard problem. It’s a cool problem, but it’s a different problem. And the second is putting the model inside a robot and having the robot being able to navigate the world. And these problems are closely related. I would argue that you need understanding to get a very effective version of the other two, but here on the West Coast, I actually see very little talk of internal representations and interpretability in the context of world models. As you said, it’s usually in the context of language, and I would argue that an agent that’s able to navigate the world, as with the second West Coast definition, or even the first, to generate a physically plausible world, that you need to have an understanding, you need to be looking at the internal representations, and I would even argue—this is an even stronger claim, and a lot of neuroscientists would disagree with me—but I would argue that the world model in the East Coast definition needs to be a functional homomorphism with the physical world. Drew: What does that mean? Joseph: A one-to-one mapping on the physical world in a functional way, in the sense where, for example, in the physical world, say I have to throw a ball in the air and catch it, there would be an internal representation inside the neural net tracking that in a way that’s interpretable and legible. And I’m gonna make a series of increasingly stronger claims, and I can imagine some of the more research oriented people might have reason to disagree, but I, based off evidence we’ve seen, this is the direction I think things are going, where if you’re to throw a ball in the air and catch it, inside the body of the world model itself, if the world model is highly accurate, performant, data efficient, there will be a very clean representation of the ball being thrown up in the air and caught. And this is why I think you need interpretability to have world models. You need to be looking at their internal representations. You need to be using that to guide training for data efficiency, for performance, and also for reliability and physical safety and security, which is a whole topic. And I would argue that no one’s really thinking about it this way. Drew: So, what is the strongest version of this claim that you subscribe to? Joseph: You need interpretability to have world models is the strongest claim, and I would argue you need interpretability to have accurate world models, data efficient world models, and reliable world models. Drew: I see, I see. So on the West Coast, when we talk about world models, often what we mean is it’s a video model. It’s generating videos, and maybe they are physically realistic or physically plausible. Or we mean we want to have some kind of generative model that can act as the brain of a robot, or can generate simulated environments to train a robot in. You’re saying the East Coast definition is more inflected by this history of neuroscience, almost. Joseph: Absolutely. Drew: What does a world model mean to someone on the East Coast then who is thinking about it from more of a neuroscience perspective? Joseph: Yeah, it would mean an agent, or you could think the brain, a foundation model that understands the world to the point its internal representations are disentangled and causal. So, for example, if there’s a ball being thrown into the air and it comes down, there’s an internal representation of the ball that is disentangled from other things inside the mind of that agent, that person, that foundation model, opposed to some conflationary set of heuristics or memorizations or shortcuts, which arguably most of our current world models still have. Drew: Do you think that sort of people’s minds have world models in this sense, where there are factorized representations or specific representations of these different physical concepts, or are we relying on this loose collection of heuristics that changes task to task? Joseph: It depends on the task. I’d say, for most physical tasks, yes. I would say humans are often very conflationary reasoners. When you get into the whole world of stereotypes and biases, this is actually not having disentangled and causal representations. This is having highly correlational heuristics. So a superhuman intelligence, I think, would have highly disentangled internal representations. Drew: So say I’m with you that in order to be a good world model, you would have these disentangled representations somewhere in the brain of that model. Why is it important that we be able to find them? Why do we have to do interpretability to make sure that they’re actually in there or that we’ve found them in the right place? Joseph: Yeah, so there are a variety of reasons. One to start with might be safety or reliability. If you could think of one of these robots in your home, we may want to test that this robot, its foundation model brain, has reliable representations of the physical world. So one example is object permanence, this water bottle. If I look away and look back, we want that representation of the water bottle to stay. We want to test that that foundation model or that agent has these understandings of physical plausibility. And with a white box analysis, you can probe inside the model to see if there are certain representations that correspond to physical plausibility. For example, there might be a manifold or some kind of feature that corresponds to object permanence, unlike various other properties of the physical world that would be harder to find with black box evaluation alone. So, combining white box evaluation to make sure that the information is there and doesn’t—sometimes it might appear and then in the middle of the net it might start disappearing to make sure yeah—to make sure that information is there is very necessary. So the example I gave was in robots in our homes, but there’s also surgical robotics as well. We want to make sure that these models are reliable and we want to be probing them for the qualities we care about at every part of the net. Drew: So when you say black box, you mean sort of strictly relying on inputs and outputs and looking at the outward behavior of the model. When you say white box, you’re talking about interpreting the internals, trying to understand the computation that’s going on under the hood that makes up these models. Is that right? Joseph: That’s exactly right. Drew: Okay, so evaluation is one reason it would be really great to have interpretability. Basically, we can evaluate and make sure that the model is understanding the right thing at the right time, and that means it’s not going to take some unwanted or unpredicted action. Are there other reasons interpretability is really important here? Joseph: Yeah, one is data efficiency. Currently, these models are extremely expensive to train, and one analogy I think of is imagine you’re in school and you have a huge test tomorrow and you’re cramming for that test and you just cram for six hours. When you actually go to take the test, you might perform okay, but the information in your mind might be kind of disorganized and you might make some errors and you might not truly understand what’s going on. And I would argue that the way we’re training a lot of these models now is kind of analogous to that. While in contrast, interpretability guided training is actually checking at various time points if the model has learned a certain behavior, for example, object permanence, and if it hasn’t, feeding in more data in a loop that encourages the learning of certain capabilities at certain times in a way that might consume orders of magnitude less data. Similarly, there’s this idea of influence functions given a capability, which data elicited that capability and where in the weights is it stored, and these are fundamentally interpretability questions. So maybe another analogy is you can imagine in a utopia or in a dystopia where we really care about the learning of children, maybe we can have some kind of fMRI as they’re learning from a textbook, and if their neural correlates are corresponding to patterns that map to understanding, this is good. And if they’re not, maybe we can intervene and be like, hey, this is clearly not working. Let’s give the kid a new textbook, or let’s do something a little bit different. And I’d say interpretability-informed training is very similar. Drew: Yeah, even without going that far as fMRI’s, or intervening— Joseph: Not to make it too sci-fi. Drew: Sure but even that—the distinction that you’re pointing to I think is very intuitive. I think people understand the difference between learning a subject from the ground up in say a college course with a really good teacher and a good textbook and you start from the foundations you learn the key concepts and then you layer on new information on top of that. Compared to this mode of learning, where you just encounter ideas here and there, they’re all kind of disparate. You don’t know how they’re related, and then on your own, you wind up making connections sometimes, you realize that two concepts were more related than you previously thought, but you were treating them as these two separate heuristics all along. It feels very intuitive, that distinction that you’re pointing to. We might want to learn in the more comprehensive way, where we’re making sure the right concepts make it into the neural network or the brain of the model. Joseph: Yeah, absolutely. And I’m not sure how much you want to dive into this, but I would also argue that there are other paradigms of making these models interpretable by design as well. And here’s where we’ll see things on a case to case basis. So let’s go back to the self-driving car example. There are certain things in a policy network here that you might care to verify that this network has learned. For example, does it have stable representations of acceleration, velocity, mass? These basic aspects of physics. There is a paradigm in which you can bake into the model certain latent variables that correspond to what you actually care about in the physical world, and now instead of randomly probing the model, which in some ways is a search problem, is a large latent space, and you’re just probing the latent space to see if there are certain properties that you care about, you know where to probe. So I think we will see a resurgence of this. It sounds a little inductive biasy, which is a little unfashionable in this bitter lesson period, but my response to that is first, I think there’s a way to find inductive biases in a way that’s unsupervised, which makes it not as handcrafted as the initial paradigm, and the second is I think we’ll need to do more and more of this, given how expensive things are right now and how data scarce some of these environments are. Drew: I want to unpack more of what you mean about the bitter lesson point in a second, but I guess just to push back on the self-driving point, I would say we have self-driving cars that are moving into the world now, and I don’t know that they’ve had to rely on these kinds of baked-in concepts. I think they’ve been learned in more of an end-to-end kind of deep learning way. What would you say to that? Has that worked? Will it continue to work? Joseph: I’d say it depends on how fast you want your development cycle to be. Drew: Okay. Joseph: If you want a really long development cycle and you want to spend a long time verifying these things, then eventually, sure, you can do these methods. But if you want to cut development costs by an order of magnitude, then these techniques become quite important. And I’d argue a lot of the self-driving car companies are hiring mechanistic interpretability researchers now to do just that. Drew: Yeah. Joseph: It could always be much better. Drew: Yeah. So let me see if I’m understanding your point about the bitter lesson correctly. The bitter lesson is this idea from Rich Sutton that general purpose methods like learning and search that scale with compute, time and time again outperform biases that we plant into a model while it’s learning. Where we sort of assume a model that does well at this task really ought to know this concept, or it ought to model some object in this way. The general purpose methods, just throwing more compute at it and just learning, tend to outperform those. But here you’re proposing that there are some concepts that a model ought to have represented somewhere, like velocity, direction, mass, and so you’re saying you think that you can defend that approach and say that should withstand the bitter lesson or should be compatible with the bitter lesson somehow. Joseph: Yeah, I think it’s compatible with the bitter lesson. I’m obviously not saying the bitter lesson is wrong. I think it just depends: do you want to train your model for 10 years or 10 weeks? Drew: Sure. Joseph: And if you think about it, our brain is an inductive bias that’s been optimized for evolution. There are certain inductive biases that are just incredibly useful to have to navigate your environment. And if you can figure out what those inductive biases are and then bake it into the architecture, then you have huge performance gains. So it’ll depend on your task. And I also think going back to the handcrafted, I’m going to top down figure out what the system cares about. I also think that’s not correct either. The paradigm I see is one, and this is very experimental, but it looks something that’s similar to distillation. But in the context of interpretability, so imagine we train our giant unsupervised video model this old-fashioned bitter lesson way, and then we treat the latent space like a world, and we navigate that world with RL to find internal representations that are A: interpretable, meaning we as humans can understand them—for example, some internal representation of velocity, if we care about that. And B: are causally relevant to the output—so it’s actually, that representation is actually recruited during the forward pass and used when the model is making some kind of decision. Is there a part of your brain that’s representing your couch, gravity, object permanence, and etc. Okay, so now let’s go back to the paper. We were asking, do video models have these disentangled representations internally? Meaning that if there’s a representation of velocity, I can control the direction of a ball. What we found in JEPA is first, a lot of the language assumptions break. Controversial, I’m not sure for these highly general physical principles like velocity, sparse autoencoders, which the language world was obsessed with for a while, are that important. I’m not convinced superposition is that important. We’re seeing these giant high-dimensional hyperspheres that are 60 dimensions floating about in latent space, and it’s also a highly entangled latent space. For example, if you’re to steer the direction of a ball that’s moving in latent space, direction is represented as this 60-dimensional circular hypersphere thing. It’s definitely not a linear feature direction. And when you steer the direction of the ball, you also end up impacting speed in a way that, like, okay, maybe train a sparse auto encoder and disentangle them, but this is difficult to do when a sparse autoencoder is in linear directions and you’re dealing with these large entities. Potentially, you could take a manifold approach, but a lot of this still needs to be researched and empirically showed out, and it hasn’t been yet. A lot of the research I’m describing came out in the last few weeks, the last few months. So what does this all mean? Why do we care? This suggests that current world models are learning highly entangled latent spaces. It’s possible this can be solved by scale. It’s possible anything can be solved by scale. It’ll just take like 20 years and be highly inefficient and consume 20 nuclear reactors of compute, and it’s also possible that if we care about direction and speed, as we might in a self-driving car, we can do what we talked about earlier by pre-baking these things into a next-generation foundation model and train it at one thousandth the cost. Drew: Okay, that’s a great explanation. Just to come back to what you’re saying about sparse autoencoders. So that’s a technique that’s popular for interpreting language models, where we say we think that at every given moment in time, when the model is thinking, it’s thinking about just a few concepts at once, and we train a separate AI model, it’s called sparse autoencoder that tries to identify what those few concepts are at any given time, assuming that each one of them is represented linearly, like in a straight line somewhere in the model’s brain. And this seems to sometimes work in some ways for language models. But you’re saying when we have this video model, we’re finding things that are not at all linear. It’s a 60-dimensional hypersphere. And it’s also kind of conflated with other physical concepts. Maybe you could kind of disentangle them if you insisted that they must be linear in a similar way where we approach language models. But then something would be lost. You’d lose some of that rich physical representation inside. Is that right? Joseph: Yeah, that’s generally right. With some nuances, first, I think in language people are finding a lot of features in language are also not linear. But in language, you can get away with linearity for longer. And maybe this is a hot take, but I think linear is the most efficient thing, and language is somewhat optimized to be linear because languages are efficient abstractions of the physical world that we use to communicate. I think in the physical world, even in the world of vision, very quickly you realize you can’t get away with linear steering. It breaks immediately. While in language, it might break after, I don’t know, several months. So we’re like, “Wait, this is a little weird. Some things are steering and some things aren’t. I wonder why?” And what you said earlier about—I’m so sorry. What was— Drew: That something would be lost maybe if we try to disentangle these or? Joseph: Yeah, well, it’s not clear, honestly, I’d say that’s an open question. Drew: But you conclude in the paper that overall most of the representations you find are task specific, not these universal factorized representations. Is that right, or so is the evidence mixed here? Joseph: There needs to be more research. This is the first study. We were looking at two different data distributions that were generated by two very different physics simulators. So it’s not clear is there some physics simulator or data distribution difference, and also is it due to the fact that we were looking at a relatively small model and generality might emerge in larger models. So that’s what that paper concludes. But this needs to be a longer research program. Drew: Okay, and you also find that there’s a “physics emergence zone” in these models. Can you explain what that means? Joseph: Yeah. So basically, the way this paper was framed is we needed some operationalization of physics, and physics is a very broad and general thing, just about the general governing dynamics of our world. So we used a task called the possible versus impossible task, which comes from cognitive science, where you have these tasks in which physics are violated. So you might, for example, have a ball go behind a wall and then just not come out the other end, and this is impossible. And the idea is that by measuring the model’s performance on these tasks, ideally, it should not be able to predict things that are impossible. You’re able to get a proxy for how well the model has internalized the rules of physics. And we use this task as a proxy for figuring out where in the model, if we look at it from a layer by layer point of view, physics emerges. Physics defined in this kind of high level way, but it’s a useful starting point. And we discover that physics seems to—as operationalized in this way—increases one third throughout the model, and it peaks in the middle of the model, and then it actually degrades if you’re to linearly decode it. And what we found is that the model is basically processing information very similar to human brains, and it’s using retinotopic coding. So it’s able to process speed and acceleration relatively quickly, but direction takes a while, and direction seems to be driving the physics emergence zone. And we notice some really interesting things in the physics emergent zone. We notice that the MLP units almost perfectly specialize in a 360 tiling in a way where every MLP neuron corresponds to a different direction of the ball in a way that’s very beautiful, combined with this blooming of very local attention heads that seem to be doing very local spatial temporal integration, that’s pretty key for how the model is processing direction of the ball, and that seems to be driving the physics emergence zone. You could maybe call it the direction emergence zone as well, but you need a sense of direction to compute most of physics. And you find yourself in this really interesting intellectual terrain of physical reasoning and neuroscience, where it’s like, how do humans do this? And it seems like models are doing something very similar. So doubling down on that intellectual lineage I think will just unlock a lot of safety insights and models as well. Drew: It also makes me wonder how LLMs do this. This understanding that we have now of the structures that emerge in the video models and the function of those structures. How does that compare to our understanding of how language models work? Joseph: Yeah, I mean, it’s a good question. I, short answer is I am less of a language interpret person, but it seems like language models are dealing with very different problems, right? You don’t have to necessarily construct the representation of direction in quite the same way. I mean, maybe you can make some toy example where you take this video, these video clips, and you turn them all into pixels, and you feed that into a language model through some tokenizer, and you see if the language model can solve the task. But I just think language models are dealing with fundamentally different problems than physical reasoning, and physical reasoning is a fundamentally different category than what language models are usually trained to solve. Drew: I think the thing that I’m coming back to is: coming into this, the way I framed it is there’s a lot of people that are focused on interpretability, which is a very hard problem, we already did an episode of this show dedicated to why interp is so hard. People are working on world models, which are also seen as a really hard problem. I think I had a sense of, well, if you’ve solved world models and you’ve made really reliable models, then interp is sort of maybe not necessary at that point. We should just have confidence in our world models. So you could think that you’re trying to solve two hard problems instead of just trying to solve one. But I think I’ve become convinced that there’s a way that these problems go hand in hand and actually complement each other very well. Joseph: Yeah, I mean they’re two sides of the same coin. Or I would say unlocking interpretability unlocks world models, in that your models are more accurate, data efficient, and reliable. Drew: Yeah, and then useful as a result. Joseph: And useful, absolutely. Drew: Cool. All right. Well, thank you so much, Sonia, for coming on the show. Joseph: Thank you so much. This has been super fun. Drew: That was Sonia Joseph. Sonia is the co-founder and CEO of World Mechanics. I’m your host, Rocket Drew. You’ve been listening to the Informations AI Deep Dive. Tune in next time.

title: Palo Alto Networks CEO Advises Daughter on New AI-Focused Venture Capital Fund
content: These days, raising a new venture fund can seem like an uphill battle. First-time managers are competing with much bigger funds that can lure founders with rich valuations—as well as track records that can wow limited partners. But what if you had unfettered access to some sage advice from a seasoned investor and executive? That’s the case for Ayesha Arora-Hughes, the daughter of Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora. Ayesha is raising her own VC fund, Permanent Partners Collective Fund I, according to a securities filing and people with knowledge of the matter—and she counts Nikesh as an adviser to the firm, one of the people said. Ayesha is targeting raising over $100 million for the fund to back AI companies, from startups developing AI applications to those making the infrastructure that powers and runs AI, one of the people said. And she’s already made her first investment, the person added, though which startup she backed couldn’t be learned. Nikesh has plenty of experience with startups and investment firms. Before joining Palo Alto Networks, he served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank when the Japanese conglomerate made an effort to invest in emerging markets like India, backing companies including ride-hailing service Ola and e-commerce marketplace Snapdeal. He’s now the chair and CEO of Palo Alto Networks, a frequent buyer of startups. Most recently, Nikesh has been on the hunt for new cybersecurity startups , a search undergirded by the belief that the sophistication of AI agents will reshape how companies protect their IT systems against cyberthreats. And in April, megafund General Catalyst appointed Nikesh to serve as the firm’s first lead independent director on its board. Ayesha previously worked at VC firm S32, which she left in July, and has invested in companies including coding agent Factory , legal tech startup Legora and chip designer Etched, according to her LinkedIn. Ayesha isn’t the first child of a tech executive to launch their own investment firm. In 2023, Reed Jobs, the eldest son of late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, founded his own venture fund, Yosemite , to focus on investments in cancer-related startups. Jobs’ VC firm , now three years old, initially set out to raise $400 million and has accumulated $1.2 billion in assets under management, according to data firm PitchBook. title: At Apple, Pigs Are About to Fly
content: Apple sure takes its own sweet time. On Monday, the company sent out invitations to a product announcement happening next Wednesday, which the company’s marketing chief teased in a message on X : “Can’t wait to pro and tell next week.” That’s likely a reference to a new MacBook Pro from the company, which Bloomberg has reported will be Apple’s first touchscreen laptop. Apparently pigs really do fly. For over a decade, Apple has treated touchscreen laptops like some kind of mutant offspring of computers and tablets, a category it had zero interest in. On a 2012 earnings call, Apple’s then-CEO Tim Cook had a memorable response to a question about the growing number of touchscreen Windows laptops coming on the market: “You can converge a toaster and a refrigerator, but those things are probably not going to be pleasing to the user.” “We’re not going to that party,” Cook added. A number of things have changed since then. Touchscreens have become somewhat normalized as laptop features. About one in every five notebook computers sold has such capabilities, by one estimate . More recently, Cook handed off the Apple CEO baton to John Ternus, a longtime hardware engineering executive who is much more of a product guy than his predecessor. Clearly, a new touchscreen laptop had to have been in the works long before Apple’s leadership transition. Still, it wouldn’t be a surprise to learn that Ternus’ rising stature within the company had something to do with it. Whoever was behind the decision, the first wave of products from the Ternus administration—the iPhone Duo foldable smartphone, HomeView smart display and now possibly a touchscreen MacBook—seems to be sending the message that Apple is ready to embrace categories it previously ignored. That’s a good thing. In Other News Elon Musk pledged to give every child in the U.S. one share of SpaceX stock next year, a gift that could be worth almost $11 billion in total. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security ordered all federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek from their computer systems and bars those agencies from making future purchases from DeepSeek. Federal prosecutors accused the former OpenAI employee who allegedly bugged the company’s offices of having ties to the Saudi royal family. title: Altman Describes Three Endgames for AI, Including One Where a Single Firm ‘Melts Everyone Else’s GPUs’
content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman last week told employees about three proposals the industry has discussed for how to safely develop AI, a stark framing that comes just as the Trump administration sets up its first system for policing “superintelligence” developers like OpenAI. One path involved developing an international organization, similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency, that would enforce safety standards, a scenario Altman appeared to support, said two people with knowledge of the comments. Another option would involve merging all of the AI labs into a single body to develop new AI safely. Altman described a third scenario—which he didn’t prefer—in which one AI developer would obtain enough economic power that it could deprive all other developers, including those that could be dangerous, of computing resources, ensuring that they couldn’t catch up, these people said. “Obviously I think that one’s terrible,” Altman said, adding that he was including it for “completeness,” according to a person with knowledge of the comment. Altman has said internally that there are too few viable proposals for how to introduce a so-called speed limit on the development of the technology. He also said he wanted humans to maintain control of the technology and to avoid scenarios in which power in the industry is too concentrated. Altman made the latest comments at a time when some AI researchers, including at OpenAI, have become increasingly anxious about whether companies at the forefront of the technology have the right systems to prevent it from going rogue or being misused for cyberattacks and other potential harms. Those concerns followed a spate of AI-powered breaches by OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, whose models broke into or compromised the systems of other companies or their own systems, even when the models understood that they weren’t supposed to take such actions. In the wake of those breaches, OpenAI has been in an all-hands-on-deck mode to develop new systems so it can launch its next major model safely. The internal concerns are particularly acute at OpenAI. Some of the company’s staff have privately questioned its commitment to safety after it fired three safety-focused researchers for allegedly improperly sharing information with an outside organization. While the Trump administration’s approach to AI oversight has focused on extracting voluntary agreements from developers like OpenAI to let the administration to review new models before they are released publicly, the Pentagon’s Emil Michael told The Information that the administration is open to more stringent checks on these companies if they behave like “drunk drivers” and put people or businesses in harm’s way. Those punishments include the kind of export controls Trump imposed on Anthropic in June, after the government became concerned about potential “jailbreak” vulnerabilities in its most advanced model, Fable. The export controls prompted the company to temporarily shut off access to the model. While the first two options Altman shared with staff would require an immense amount of coordination between companies or governments, Altman said OpenAI can’t afford to give up ground to rivals at the moment, these people said. Both OpenAI and its main rival Anthropic are moving quickly towards initial public offerings. But in the next year, OpenAI needs to decide which of these paths it wants to push for, Altman said. Altman’s comments highlight the dilemma AI labs face in coordinating with rivals. For now, OpenAI, Google and Anthropic are working on a new U.S. AI safety-focused group, the Standards Authority for Frontier AI , that they hope to launch by the end of the year or early in 2027. The group would support independent evaluators embedded within the AI developers who would ensure safe practices and determine how developers should report safety and security incidents. However, the companies have disagreed on a number of points, including whether the new organization or an outside body should conduct safety and capability testing of new models. Anthropic also has begun to push its own AI safety agenda to U.S. policymakers. The company recently pitched lawmakers on a draft bill which proposed allowing the Commerce Department to stop an AI lab from training or using a new model if the AI could cause more than $1 billion in damages or the death or serious injury of more than 50 people. The proposed bill also would require AI labs to hire independent safety evaluators who would assess models at least twice a year. Some AI leaders have argued that new regulations or testing-focused agencies would only further entrench the incumbent developers—namely, Anthropic and OpenAI. Executives such as Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang say such regulations would impose overly burdensome rules on up-and-coming developers, a concept known as regulatory capture. IAEA or CERN Altman and other leaders at OpenAI have been pushing publicly for a body modeled on the International Atomic Energy Agency for years. In May 2023, Altman, along with OpenAI co-founder and president Greg Brockman and then-chief scientist Ilya Sutskever, published a blog post arguing that the industry would likely need “something like an IAEA for superintelligence efforts” that would be able to inspect systems, require audits and track compute and energy usage. The IAEA-esque body would require international cooperation from all countries that are developing state-of-the-art models, including China. Last month, Chinese president Xi Jinping acknowledged the dangers of AI, saying that China and the U.S. have the “capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people.” It’s unclear how much China is willing to work together with the U.S. towards this aim. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent proposed a new AI safety “notification mechanism” during talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng last month, but Chinese officials have not yet officially agreed to the framework. Similar to OpenAI, Anthropic leaders have also proposed international cooperation, including with China, as a potential solution to AI safety concerns. In a September essay, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote that he believes it’s possible for the U.S. and China to agree on certain criteria, like prohibiting narrow and clearly dangerous uses of AI such as making biological weapons and testing for risks in areas like cybersecurity. Unlike OpenAI, though, Anthropic has been much more aggressive in arguing that the U.S. should maintain a significant lead in AI development over China and take steps like banning the sales of advanced chips in China to keep that lead. To OpenAI staff last week, Altman described the second path for developing safe AI as the “Demis plan,” a reference to a prior proposal from Demis Hassabis, then the leader of Alphabet’s DeepMind AI lab. About a decade ago, Hassabis proposed creating an organization similar to CERN, the particle physics lab jointly controlled by dozens of countries to pursue cutting edge research. In Altman’s version of the Hassabis proposal, major AI firms would effectively merge into or produce work through a single entity that would provide new models to countries that work with it. It’s unclear whether Hassabis’ version of a “CERN for AI” would have gone as far as Altman’s spin on the concept. More recently, Hassabis has pushed for a self-regulatory body similar to the U.S. Financial Industry Regulatory Authority. ‘Eliezer Plan’ Altman referred to the third option as the “Eliezer plan,” the people said, a reference to Eliezer Yudkowsky, a well-known AI safety theorist and advocate with ties to key members of Anthropic. Yudkowsky has long argued that advanced AI systems pose an existential risk to humanity. Yudkowsky said in a blog post in 2022 that whoever develops superintelligence first will need to use it to perform a “pivotal act”—an intervention that would prevent other people and organizations from developing dangerous superintelligence. One such intervention could involve destroying the AI chips that other developers use. Altman said this moment could occur when an AI developer attains recursive self-improvement, AI that’s able to improve itself, and using the resulting economic might to “melt everyone else’s GPUs.” (OpenAI and other developers say they are intently focused on achieving such RSI.) Altman has characterized this path as an attempt to centralize and control advanced AI under a single company—a future Altman said he didn’t want. Given Yudkowsky’s connections to Anthropic, the comment was viewed as a subtle dig at Anthropic, said one of the people with knowledge of it.

title: The Information Announces New OpenAI, Google, Finance and Asia Reporters
content: The Information is pleased to announce new reporters who will carry on the publication’s rich track record of reporting exclusive news on the most important people and companies in business. They’ll report on OpenAI, Google, Asia and finance. Jemima McEvoy , OpenAI Jemima McEvoy is changing roles to take on the OpenAI beat. In just over a year at The Information writing for the Weekend section, Jemima has proven herself to be a resourceful, industrious and sharp-eyed reporter with a flair for colorful features and a knack for breaking news. Her run of illuminating stories includes profiles of Epstein-linked investor Masha Bucher , Midjourney founder David Holz and ultra-secretive investor Zach Frankel . An adept collaborator, she also co-authored great reads on OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife Anna , Sequoia’s leadership duo and Anthropic “first lady” Cami Clark —not to mention The Information’s inaugural 50 Most Influential People in Tech list. And she has helped deliver scoops on Valar Atomics and Shield AI and deconstructed trends such as the rise of padel . Jemima joined The Information after five years at Forbes, where she made her bones writing about billionaires and their businesses. She has also interned for CBS News and was editor-in-chief of Washington Square News, the independent student newspaper at her alma mater, New York University. Ryan Barwick , Google Ryan Barwick is joining us to cover Google. Ryan comes to us from Axios, where he spent the past year-and-a-half delivering exclusives as a consumer-industry deal reporter for Axios Pro. Ryan cut his reporting teeth covering advertising technology, giving him a deep understanding of the economic engine that has long powered Google’s core business. Before Axios, he was the senior reporter for Morning Brew’s advertising vertical, where he landed scoops on companies including Meta, Amazon and Twitter as well as Google, and covered the search giant’s battle with regulators. Prior to that, he wrote about the ad industry at Adweek, was a broadcast associate at CBS News and covered the intersection of policy and technology as a fellow at the Center for Public Integrity. Claudia Chong, AI and Data Centers (Asia) Claudia is covering the intensifying AI race from Singapore, where both Chinese and U.S. tech companies are staffing up. She also may report on topics including chip smuggling, crypto and anything else she digs up. Claudia joins us from S-RM, a UK-based risk advisory firm where she specialized in APAC disputes, investigations, and corporate due diligence. Prior to that, she worked on ByteDance’s LLM training operations in Singapore and spent nearly six years as a correspondent at The Business Times, the premier business publication in Southeast Asia, covering venture capital, tech, and private wealth across the region. Her journalistic work earned her a Singapore Press Holdings (SPH) Media Award for Excellence in 2024 for the investigation into Singapore’s largest money laundering scandal. Beyond training LLMs and conducting due diligence, her skills also extend to M&A, having conducted research that helped with the SPH’s acquisition of the Tech in Asia publication in 2024. Alex Eichenstein , Tech Capital Markets We’re excited to announce that Alex Eichenstein is joining the finance team, covering tech capital markets. Alex comes to us from The Deal, where she spent more than two and a half years covering healthcare deals. She regularly broke PE acquisition news while also writing deeper dives on major investing shifts, including how buyout firms’ struggles to find exits for practice rollups fueled a shift toward health tech investments. We’re excited for Alex to help deepen our finance coverage in her new role, focusing on the fast-evolving debt and equity markets and deals redefining how tech companies fund themselves. Alex is a graduate of Columbia Journalism School and worked as a social media editor at Protocol prior to that.

title: How DeepSeek Is Shaping Huawei’s AI Chips in a Growing Challenge to Nvidia
content: DeepSeek is working closely with Huawei Technologies to shape the design of future AI chips, two people familiar with the matter said, in a collaboration that could help China build frontier AI models without Nvidia’s technology. The relationship goes beyond the kinds of conversations companies have with chip suppliers about their semiconductor road maps. Huawei engineers are incorporating DeepSeek’s requests and suggestions into design decisions, such as how models calculate and move data between processors, for chips that will come out next year and beyond, the people said. To do this work, the Huawei engineers have been stationed at DeepSeek’s offices for an extended period, one of the people said. The extensive collaboration, which hasn’t previously been reported, brings two of China’s most important tech companies into a unified effort on an issue central to Beijing’s technology strategy. China’s government wants the country’s AI built on homegrown chips and has limited how many Nvidia processors China’s largest tech companies can buy. Huawei already leads the country’s AI chip market, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC in May that his company had “largely conceded” the market to domestic rivals. In particular, the cooperation could help China crack one of the biggest impediments to fully homegrown AI: the powerful chips needed to train new models quickly. Despite attempts by both the Chinese and U.S. governments to limit Chinese companies’ access to Nvidia chips, China’s top AI developers still train their best models on chips from the U.S. company , sometimes obtained through smuggling. If the collaboration yields a Huawei chip that DeepSeek can use to fully train a top-tier model, other Chinese AI labs could follow suit. Last month, DeepSeek founder Liang Wenfeng told investors at a meeting that using more Chinese chips for training was a major priority, The Information reported . DeepSeek is planning to start using Huawei’s current flagship AI chip, the recently released Ascend 950DT, for pre-training—the stage where a model learns its basic abilities from vast amounts of data over weeks or months—as soon as the end of this year, according to one of the two people and a separate person with direct knowledge of the effort. Tests are still underway and the timetable could change, they said. Huawei, meanwhile, is planning to give DeepSeek most of the supply of the Ascend 960DT, its next training chip, when it comes out next year, rather than spreading it across China’s AI developers. DeepSeek plans to use it both to train models and to run them, one of the two people said. Huawei has said it will release a new generation of Ascend chips annually, including the 960DT in the first quarter of 2027, the 970 in 2028 and the 980 in 2029. Hurdles to China’s Chip Efforts The chip effort still faces significant obstacles, including constraints on how quickly Huawei’s manufacturing partner can ramp up production to levels needed for the large chip clusters used to train models. U.S. export controls have made that harder, with Washington blocking Huawei from using the world’s top chip manufacturer, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., in 2020 and limiting China’s access since 2024 to the advanced high-bandwidth memory AI chips require. And even with DeepSeek’s help, it will likely be a while before Huawei’s chips rival the power of Nvidia’s. The U.S. company’s B300 chips deliver roughly seven times the raw arithmetic performance of Huawei’s Ascend 950, according to research institute Epoch AI , which expects Huawei to stay three to four years behind Nvidia on single-chip performance through 2030. While Huawei’s weaker chips make models slower to build, they come from a supplier that U.S. export rules can’t control. DeepSeek is choosing to “go a little slower but go a lot longer,” said Qingyuan Lin, a senior analyst at Bernstein who covers China’s chip industry. Only a few companies have trained frontier models on non-Nvidia chips, including Google on its own tensor processing units and Anthropic on Google TPUs and Amazon chips. Previously, DeepSeek used Huawei chips for running its models and for post-training—the stage of refining a pre-trained model for reasoning and other tasks. DeepSeek isn’t walking away from Nvidia. It is trying to access more of Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips, along with older Nvidia processors, one of the two people said. Blackwell chips are barred from export to China, but DeepSeek has obtained them anyway and used them to train its V4 models, The Information reported . Intermediaries bought Blackwell servers in countries where sales are allowed and set them up in data centers that passed inspection. The servers were then taken apart and the chips shipped to China. Nvidia’s Lock-In Loosens A key component of DeepSeek’s effort with Huawei chips is TileLang, an open-source programming language built by a team led by Peking University researchers and released in January 2025. It lets engineers write small programs known as kernel code that carry out an AI model’s calculations with less code than older methods require. TileLang is an alternative to writing code directly in CUDA, Nvidia’s widely used programming system for its graphics processing units, and can run on different chips. DeepSeek first used TileLang with Nvidia GPUs, publishing TileLang code alongside versions written in CUDA when the Chinese company released an experimental V3.2 model in September 2025. TileLang now handles most of those programs in model development for DeepSeek’s V4 models. Last month, DeepSeek released a version of TileLang for Huawei’s Ascend 950 chips, along with five sets of code covering the calculations and data transfers needed to run its models. It said every TileLang program it uses in training now has an Ascend version. DeepSeek said Huawei’s engineers gave “unreserved” help in building them. TileLang could further loosen Nvidia’s grip. For years, CUDA has been one of the U.S. company’s most important tools for keeping customers using its chips, because moving to another type of chip requires a long, laborious rewrite. With TileLang, code still has to be adjusted, but DeepSeek doesn’t have to start from zero when it moves work from Nvidia to Huawei chips. Huawei is taking other steps to make up for the weaker performance of its chips. The company is linking many processors into one system big enough to train models, and recently began shipping these supernodes with Ascend 950DT at high volume, the people said. Huawei Rotating Chairman Eric Xu said last month that 950DT training tests had gone well, that large-scale supply would start around the turn of the year, and that he expects many developers to train on them in 2027. He also said Huawei couldn’t meet domestic demand and was limiting overseas sales. DeepSeek’s newer tests use more than 1,000 processors, the people said. A full pre-training run could need well over 10,000 Ascend 950DTs running nonstop for weeks. One failed chip or a delay in moving data can leave the rest waiting, and repeated disruptions can derail the run. Some of the software needed to manage systems that large is still unfinished, the people said.

title: 云南能投新能源装机已达277.486万千瓦--中国能源新闻网
content:
云南能投新能源装机已达277.486万千瓦--中国能源新闻网
中国能源传媒集团有限公司主办
能源中国IOS版
云南能投新能源装机已达277.486万千瓦
衣韵潼）10月20日，云南能源投资股份有限公司（以下简称“云南能投”）公告，全资子公司马龙云能投新能源开发有限公司投建的色甲光伏发电项目于10月17日实现全容量并网发电。至此，云南能投已投产发电的新能源总装机容量达到277.486万千瓦，其中风电249.386万千瓦、光伏28.1万千瓦。
据了解，色甲光伏发电项目位于曲靖市马龙区，额定容量2万千瓦。预计投产后年均上网电量3178万千瓦时，年均等效满负荷小时数为1326小时。项目不设升压站，以1回35千伏集电线路接入通泉风电场扩建项目110千伏升压站35千伏侧Ⅱ段母线送出，是云南能投在马龙区域投运的第五个规模化绿色能源项目。
云南能投表示，色甲光伏发电项目全容量并网发电是公司在双碳背景下积极践行国家和云南省能源发展战略、构建以新能源为主体的新型电力系统的重要举措，有利于进一步提升公司新能源装机规模，促进新能源主业的做强做优做大，增强核心竞争力。同时，对促进当地经济发展，助力云南省双碳目标实现亦有积极意义。

title: 四川发布风光新能源项目竞配办法--中国能源新闻网
content:
四川发布风光新能源项目竞配办法--中国能源新闻网
中国能源传媒集团有限公司主办
能源中国IOS版
四川发布风光新能源项目竞配办法
为规范全省风光新能源资源开发秩序，构建统一规范、公开透明、竞争有序的市场化配置机制，10月19日，四川省发展改革委印发《四川省新能源资源市场化配置管理办法》，规定市场化配置方法、程序、评审标准，项目开发权管理与履约要求。文件如下：
关于印发《四川省新能源资源市场化配置管理办法》的通知（川发改能源规〔2026〕434号）
各市（州）发展改革委（能源局、办），成都市经济和信息化局、达州市能源产业发展局，省级有关部门，国家能源局四川监管办，国网四川省电力公司，有关能源企业：
为规范全省风光新能源资源开发秩序，构建统一规范、公开透明、竞争有序的市场化配置机制，根据国家有关法律法规和国家光伏、风电资源开发管理规定，结合我省实际，省发展改革委、省能源局组织制定了《四川省新能源资源市场化配置管理办法》，现予印发，请遵照执行。
四川省发展和改革委员会 四川省能源局
四川省新能源资源市场化配置管理办法
第一条为规范全省新能源资源开发秩序，构建统一规范、公开透明、竞争有序的市场化配置机制，依据《中华人民共和国能源法》《中华人民共和国可再生能源法》《企业投资项目核准和备案管理条例》《光伏电站开发建设管理办法》《风电开发建设管理暂行办法》等法律法规，结合四川省实际，制定本办法。
第二条本办法适用于四川省行政区域内集中式风电、集中式光伏（含光热）电站的资源统筹、主体遴选、开发权授予及全周期履约等监督管理。
全省新能源资源实行省级统一管理、总量统筹，坚持源网协同、科学有序推进，优先保障省人民政府确定的重大战略工程、重点产业项目。
第三条新能源资源市场化配置应当遵循以下原则：
（一）省级统筹、分级负责。根据省人民政府授权，省发展改革委（省能源局）负责全省集中式风电、光伏（光热）电站的资源开发权归口管理、统筹调控和审核监督工作；地方人民政府或其授权的能源主管部门负责项目谋划、组织配置、属地初审及日常监督管理。
（二）公开公平、竞争择优。健全竞争择优工作机制，全面推行市场化配置，坚持公开公平、公正透明，保障各类市场主体平等准入、公平竞争，鼓励民营企业平等参与。不得实施定向配置、协议配置等。
（三）生态优先、依法合规。严守生态保护红线，遵守生态环境分区管控要求，履行水土保持、植被恢复、生态修复等生态环境保护法定责任。严格落实行业法规政策，规范项目建设与行业监管，推动绿色低碳安全发展。
（四）属地共享、惠民利民。统筹风光新能源开发与地方发展所需，依规健全企地利益联结机制，依法保障农村集体经济组织、农牧民等主体合法权益，实现属地共享发展。
第四条严格执行以下禁止性规定：
（一）不得违规指定或变相指定经营主体，保障合规主体平等参与市场竞争；
（二）不得强制配套产业、捆绑额外投资，严禁违规收取保证金及不合理费用；
（三）不得通过特许经营、划片管控等方式圈占新能源资源；
（四）不得侵害群众、集体经济组织及市场主体合法权益，禁止强制土地流转；
（五）不得擅自拆分规划项目，不得违规干预市场化配置评审过程、增设排他性准入条件。
第二章 配置方式与规划管理
第五条集中式风电、光伏（光热）电站项目实行市场化配置，择优确定项目法人。
接入新建500千伏汇集站的集中式风电、光伏电站，装机原则上不低于10万千瓦、50万千瓦。接入现有500千伏汇集站的集中式风电、光伏电站，原则上不低于5万千瓦、10万千瓦。确因地块距离、用地条件、送出受限以及实施绿电直连等因素导致规模缩减的，按其可实施最大规模组织推进，确保规模化、集约化开发。
纳入水风光一体化基地的项目，实行基地一体化规划、一体化编制开发建设方案，坚持市场化推动、分期分批有序实施。
依托开发区、工业园区厂房建筑物及其附属场所建设且与公共电网连接点为220千伏的光伏发电项目，参照集中式光伏电站备案。产权方可采取自建或与第三方合作方式开发，项目实施方案由市（州）能源主管部门组织电网企业等单位，依据所在地电力系统的承载力评估情况进行审定，审定后向省发展改革委（省能源局）报备后组织实施。装机规模小于5万千瓦，可采取自发自用、余电上网模式，其建设运营参照大型工商业分布式光伏进行管理。
对取得矿业权的经营主体，且矿业权剩余使用年限不低于20年，符合风电、光伏发电发展规范用地管理要求及地方国土空间规划的，可利用矿权地面建设集中式光伏电站和风电。项目实施方案经市（州）审定，向省发展改革委（省能源局）报备后组织实施，开发方式可选择全额上网或绿电直连模式。
第六条省发展改革委（省能源局）会同省级自然资源、生态环境、林草等部门（单位），指导市（州）做好规划或实施方案的编制工作。资源富集的市（州）编制新能源资源规划，其他市（州）编制实施方案。规划或实施方案报省发展改革委（省能源局）审核后，由市（州）能源主管部门印发实施。
第七条  市（州）依据风光新能源规划或实施方案，编制拟配置的项目实施方案，经市（州）人民政府同意后报省发展改革委（省能源局）审核。拟配置项目应当满足以下条件：
（一）符合国土空间规划、新能源资源规划等，完成用地、用林、用草等敏感性因素排查；
（二）电网接入与消纳意见已初步落实；
（三）涉及租用农村集体土地、集体草原等建设光伏发电项目，项目所在乡（镇）、村（社区）需按规定召开村民（代表）会议，依法形成同意开发的决议。
第三章 市场化配置程序
第八条市（州）人民政府或其授权的能源主管部门组织开展市场化配置，组建竞争配置工作机构，负责编制竞配文件、发布公告、组织评审、公示结果等工作。
第九条市场化配置应当按照以下程序进行：
（一）编制方案。市（州）能源主管部门编制项目实施方案，按程序报省发展改革委（省能源局）审核。省发展改革委（省能源局）在收到方案后10个工作日内会同有关单位完成审核（不含第三方咨询评估机构评审时间）。通过审核的项目方可组织实施。
项目已纳入绿电直连整体实施方案并审核通过的，无需再次编制项目实施方案报审。
（二）发布公告。在省或市（州）公共资源交易平台发布竞配公告，公告期不少于20日。公告内容应当包括项目基本情况、申请人资格要求、评审标准、申请文件提交截止时间等。
（三）申请与资格审查。申请人按公告要求提交申请文件。竞争配置工作机构对申请人资格条件及材料完整性进行审查。申请人一般不少于3家，若申请人少于3家，应当重新开展竞配工作。重新竞配后申请人仍少于3家的，可继续按程序开展后续审查评分工作。
（四）专家评审。由7名及以上技术、经济、政策等方面的专家组成单数评审小组，行业专家比例不低于三分之二，政府部门代表不超过三分之一。行业专家从省或市（州）有关专家库中随机抽取，实行利益回避和全程留痕。同时，积极推行“评定分离”，鼓励开展异地远程评审，探索推动人工智能辅助评审。
（五）结果公示。评审结束后，通过省或市（州）公共资源交易平台公示中选候选人，公示期不少于3日。申请人对竞配过程或结果有异议的，应当在公示期内以书面形式向竞争配置工作机构提出。竞争配置工作机构应当自收到异议之日起3日内作出答复。对答复不服的，可向省发展改革委（省能源局）申请复核。
（六）确定项目法人。公示期满无异议或异议已依法处理的，市（州）人民政府将竞配结果的项目法人建议报省发展改革委（省能源局）审核确认。省发展改革委（省能源局）审核确认并向省政府报备后将结果通知市（州）人民政府。
（七）明确开发权及签订协议。地方人民政府或其授权的能源主管部门应在收到报备结果通知后30日内与中选人签订投资开发协议，明确开发权。投资开发协议主要条款应当与竞配公告及申请文件的内容一致，地方不得另行订立背离合同实质性内容的其他协议。
第十条涉及矿权重叠的项目，应当依法开展压覆矿产资源评估和生态影响评价，项目选址确与合法矿业权交叉的，由项目法人与矿业权人协商并签订书面协议后，按程序推进项目建设。
第四章 评审标准
第十一条参与市场化配置的市场主体应当具备以下基本条件：
（一）具有独立法人资格；
（二）具有良好的商业信誉和健全的财务会计制度；
（三）具有与项目投资规模相适应的资金实力和融资能力；
（四）近三年无重大违法违规记录，未被列入严重失信主体名单。
允许联合体参与竞配，联合体成员不得超过3家，签订的联合体协议应明确牵头方、出资比例及权利义务。联合体各方不得以自己名义单独或加入其他联合体参与同一项目的竞争。
第十二条市场化配置评审采用百分制综合评估法。评审指标及权重如下：
（一）企业综合实力（20分）：包括企业资质与业绩、财务实力与融资能力、信用记录与履约能力等；
（二）技术方案（30分）：包括项目设计方案先进性（设备选型与技术路线）、新能源系统友好性（新型储能合理配置情况的分数不低于5分）、建设进度与质量控制、运营维护方案等。光热发电项目可结合储热时长、调峰能力等设置技术评审指标；
（三）财务方案（20分）：包括投资估算合理性、资金筹措方案可靠性、经济效益与市场竞争力、投资决策文件等；
（四）创新与可持续发展（15分）：包括技术创新或模式创新、环境保护与社会责任、生态修复方案等；
（五）地方融合发展（15分）：包括履行属地社会责任，助力乡村振兴；优先吸纳本地劳动力就业，开展岗位技能培训，带动群众稳定增收；深化企地协同联动，探索股权合作、联合开发等共建共赢模式。
第五章 开发权管理与履约监管
第十三条开发权依据市场化配置结果依法授予。地方无正当理由逾期不签订协议，项目法人可向省发展改革委（省能源局）申请协调或依规退出。
第十四条项目法人应当按以下时限推进项目：
（一）光伏发电项目：自签订投资开发协议之日起6个月内完成备案；
（二）风电项目：自签订投资开发协议之日起18个月内完成核准；
（三）完成核准（备案）后，应当按签订的投资开发协议约定时限开工、按期建成并网。
因用地、用林用草、电网接入及不可抗力等非项目法人自身原因耽误的时间应予以扣除。
第十五条项目在授予开发权至建成投产期间内不得擅自变更投资主体和股权结构。确因兼并重组、同一集团内部调整等正当理由需要变更的，应当经省发展改革委（省能源局）同意。执行司法机关生效判决、仲裁裁决等具备正当理由需要变更的，由项目开发权承接方向省发展改革委（省能源局）报备。违反上述规定的，视为变相倒卖项目开发权。
第十六条市场主体存在以下情形之一的，依法收回开发权：
（一）逾期未备案、未核准以及未开工且无正当理由的；
（二）违反评审中作出的自愿承诺且拒不整改的；
（三）通过弄虚作假、围标串标、利益输送等不正当方式获取项目的；
（四）违规转让、倒卖项目开发权的。
第六章 监督管理与法律责任
第十七条省发展改革委（省能源局）负责对市（州）资源配置工作进行监督指导。
第十八条市（州）发展改革（能源）、自然资源、林草、生态环境等部门依据职责对资源配置活动进行监督。竞配公告、评审结果等关键信息应当及时在省或市（州）公共资源交易平台公开，接受社会监督。全省风光新能源资源市场化配置工作实行全程留痕、档案长期留存制度。
第十九条市（州）及县（市、区）政府、行业部门及公职人员违反本办法禁止性规定，违规指定主体、强制配套、垄断资源、侵害合法权益，以及擅自拆分规划项目、干预专家评审、违规设置壁垒的，由上级机关责令整改并通报，对有关责任单位、责任人员开展约谈；涉嫌违纪违法的，依纪依法移送处理。
第二十条本办法施行前印发的风光新能源开发管理相关文件，与本办法规定不一致的，以本办法为准。市（州）已发布的风光新能源资源配置相关规范性文件，应当在本办法施行后及时完成修订并向省发展改革委（省能源局）报备。
第二十一条市（州）人民政府可依据本办法制定实施细则。实施细则不得增设强制性、排他性条款，不得突破本办法规定的程序、时限和禁止性要求。
第二十二条本办法由省发展改革委（省能源局）负责解释。
第二十三条本办法自2026年11月20日起施行，有效期5年，国家另有新规定的从其规定。

title: 20亿！磷酸铁锂龙头又扩产--中国能源新闻网
content:
20亿！磷酸铁锂龙头又扩产--中国能源新闻网
中国能源传媒集团有限公司主办
能源中国IOS版
20亿！磷酸铁锂龙头又扩产
）10月19日晚间，磷酸铁锂龙头湖南裕能新能源电池材料股份有限公司（以下简称“湖南裕能”）披露投资事项，拟在湘潭当地，雨湖区鹤岭镇建设六期磷酸铁锂项目，总投资额不超过20亿元，资金来源为企业自筹。
公告指出，湘潭具备较好的电池材料产业集聚基础，产业配套完善，有利于项目生产运营。项目总建筑面积约8万平方米，建设期12个月，主要将新建生产厂房，配套建设厂区道路、用电设施、消防安防、环保处理等公用工程，并购置磷酸铁锂成套生产线设备。
“本次投资扩产符合公司战略发展规划，将进一步完善磷酸铁锂产能布局，提升核心产品供给能力，满足下游新能源汽车、储能及新兴应用领域未来业务发展和市场拓展的需要，对促进公司长期稳定发展具有重要意义。”湖南裕能表示。
近年来，磷酸铁锂作为动力电池、储能电池的核心主材，市场需求全面爆发，头部企业产能利用率均维持高位。公开资料显示，仅今年上半年，湖南裕能磷酸盐正极材料销量就达到66.72万吨，同比增长近四成，产能利用率高达95.92%。
在持续攀升的市场需求下，湖南裕能扩产步履不停。早在今年7月，就宣布投建贵州裕能（瓮安）矿化一体新能源电池材料循环产业项目，总投资额高达240亿元；此后9月下旬，再次公告将西班牙年产5万吨锂电池正极材料项目建设规模提升至7万吨/年，投资总额从9.82亿元增至16.5亿元。
“明年市场需求预计至少还会保持30%的增速，特别是高端磷酸铁锂产品的需求增速会更高。”在今年的半年度业绩说明会上湖南裕能指出，高端产品是公司近年来的重点研发方向，新建产线都是按生产高端产品的标准来设计，未来高端产品的出货占比还会进一步提升。

title: 昱能科技亮相第140届广交会&捷克智慧能源展，加速拓展海内外光储市场
content: 广州和布拉格2026年10月16日 /美通社/ -- 近日，两大国际盛会——第140届广交会与2026捷克国际智慧能源展盛大举行。昱能科技凭借其在光伏+储能领域的深厚积累与创新技术，携多场景光储解决方案及多款明星产品亮相国际双展，持续深耕海内外光储市场。广交会作为中国历史最久、规模最大、层级最高的外贸盛会，被公认为中国外贸的“超级晴雨表“，第一期“先进制造“聚焦新能源等前沿题材，是新能源企业对接全球采购商的重要窗口。昱能科技亮相第140届广交会捷克国际智慧能源展是中东欧地区最具影响力的光储展之一，为行业相关设备制造商、分销商、安装商和终端用户提供了一个良好的交流机会，也是中国光储企业展示实力、深入欧洲市场的重要平台。昱能科技亮相2026捷克智慧能源展一、第140届广交会伴随全球能源转型、碳中和深入推进，国际新能源市场合作需求日益旺盛。此次，昱能科技依托广交会的全球化开放交流平台，重点带来了微光储、户用光储解决方案及多款明星产品，具备安全可靠、智能高效、灵活便捷等显著优势，可满足光伏发电、负载供电、电力存储、能量管理等多样化需求。面向阳台DIY、户用及中小商户等场景，AC耦合储能一体机Lake-6内置6kWh储能，一体集成设计，安装便捷，支持DIY插电即用，无需改装；依托交流耦合储能技术，可以兼容EZ1系列微逆或其他品牌逆变器的光伏系统，快速实现存量光伏配储；同时该产品也能单独使用，从电网取电，实现电能充放，满足峰谷套利、自用备电等需求。让储能简单、实用且易于部署。第140届广交会外商亲切与昱能科技工作人员交流户用光储作为分布式光储的重要应用场景形式，不仅能够提高能源利用效率、降低成本，还可以提供家庭应急电力供应、保障生活质量。此次昱能科技的展台上，重点带来了交流耦合、混合耦合两大技术路线的户储产品，其中，太阳能储能混合逆变器LSH-6采用混合耦合储能技术，集光伏、储能、并网、离网、智能管理等功能于一体，不仅可以直连光伏组件与电池，实现“直流电直充电池“的高效耦合，还可以在交流侧并联接入外部光伏系统或与电网交互，能源调度更加灵活自由，一站式满足新装光伏、老旧系统升级、峰谷节电、应急供电等需求，是新建光储或存量改造光储的灵活之选。第140届广交会外商与昱能科技人员了解户用光储产品二、2026捷克国际智慧能源展近年来，捷克正依托政策与市场需求等有利条件，积极融入全球光储市场发展的大潮。此次展会，昱能科技诚意满满，携微光储、户用光储、工商业光储全场景能源方案亮相，重点带来了APstorage 261L/2000L及三相微型逆变器QT2D的工商业光储方案、AC耦合储能一体机Lake-6及三相储能逆变器ELT-12的家庭储能方案。面向工厂、园区、商业综合体等工商业大型储能场景，昱能科技重磅展示了APstorage系列储能产品——261L、2000L，依托先进、灵活的组串式储能技术，集成完善的液冷系统与消防保护系统，具有高安全、高效率、长寿命的优势，为当地工商用户提供峰谷套利、需量管理、应急供电等多元价值。其中APstorage 261L更是凭借多层硬核防护，在不久前成功通过全球公认难度极高的UL 9540A热失控蔓延测试，安全性能达到了国际领先水平，同时产品整机占地仅1.3㎡，体积紧凑，便于运输，并采用即插即用的接口设计，支持多柜体自由并机扩容，满足了欧洲市场对高效、安全、易部署的储能解决方案需求。昱能科技亮相2026捷克智慧能源展在家庭户用领域——2026年6月，捷克“新绿色补贴“（Nová zelená úsporám）将普通家庭的直接补贴转为国家贴息的免息贷款，并规定：独立住宅获贷的光伏系统必须配套锂电储能，容量不得低于装机功率（kWh≥kWp）——储能从“选配“变成“获补门槛“，成为刚需配套。此次参展的三相储能逆变器ELT-12，精准契合当地政策与市场需求，可在交流侧与家庭现有光伏系统并联接入，进行光储系统升级；采用48V低压电池输入设计，可搭配多台低压电池并联工作，以扩展存储容量；支持自发自用、备用电源、分时控制、AI调度等运行模式，实现能源灵活管理，并且具备EPS离网功能，在电网断电时也能给负载持续供电，更好满足家庭能源需求。昱能科技三相储能逆变器ELT-12亮相2026捷克智慧能源展展会既是产品与方案的展示窗口，更是思想碰撞、携手拓局的合作平台。此次双展期间，昱能科技与海内外的观众、行业专家、媒体等进行了深入的技术交流与分享，加深了与欧洲等全球市场的联系，为公司的全球化发展战略注入了新的活力。

title: 从一罐绿氢到一辆重卡 包头风光氢储产业链加速贯通
content:
秋日的达茂草原上，巨型风机叶片迎风旋转，光伏板在阳光下铺展成片。在内蒙古华电氢能科技有限公司的控制室里，屏幕上跳动的数字记录着又一批绿氢的诞生。这里生产的每一立方米氢气，都来自草原上的风和光。
“项目全程不使用网电，全部是绿电制氢。”内蒙古华电氢能科技有限公司党委委员、副总经理肖永健指着中控屏向记者介绍。这是20万千瓦风光制氢示范项目，风光配套总规模20万千瓦，其中风电12万千瓦、光伏8万千瓦，设计年产绿氢7800吨。2023年12月，企业首次制出99.999%的高纯度氢气，成为内蒙古自治区首批制氢示范项目中首个制出高纯度氢气的企业。2024年11月，企业成功实现天然气掺烧绿氢，在国内绿氢领域创下三项之“最”：国内最早实现工业天然气掺烧绿氢并运用于工业供能，实现工业天然气与绿氢最高的掺烧比例，打造2000吨/年的最大绿氢掺烧天然气规模。当前，氢气主要作为原料和燃料使用，已落地多个应用场景。
华电氢能的发展正是包头市氢能产业加速起势的生动缩影。“十四五”以来，包头市抢抓新能源发展机遇，依托风光资源富集、工业基础雄厚、应用场景广阔等优势，把氢能产业作为打造“1144”现代化产业体系的重要抓手，推动氢能“制、储、输、用”全链条发展。
在制氢端，以华电为龙头持续扩大绿氢供给规模。达茂旗20万千瓦风光制氢示范项目已稳定运行两年多，项目依托风光互补配置，除极端天气外均可全天稳定运行，解决了纯光制氢项目仅能白天生产的短板。同时，华电百万千瓦风光制氢等多个大型制氢项目也正在加快建设，绿氢供给规模持续扩大。
在储运端，白云鄂博矿区至包头市氢气长输管道工程即将投运。作为连接山北地区与山南地区的输氢管道，该项目是国家能源局首批能源领域氢能试点项目，属于内蒙古自治区“一干双环四出口”绿氢输送管网支干线，起自巴润工业园首站，终至昆都仑区末站，全长约195公里，设计压力6.3兆帕，核准年输氢量10万吨、远期可达24万吨。投运后，进一步提升绿氢连续、稳定、规模化供应能力。土右旗综合能源站已投用，搭配多座加氢撬装站，全市日加氢能力达11.6吨。
在应用端，全市绿氢应用场景加快落地、日益多元。交通领域，已投运氢能重卡160余辆、稀土固态储氢两轮车2000余辆。其中，北奔重型汽车集团有限公司牵头的“揭榜挂帅”项目核心成果——49吨300kW氢燃料电牵引车已进入批量生产与市场销售阶段。工业领域，金鄂博完成20%天然气掺氢示范，同步推进化工、氢基燃料、氢冶金等示范。从制氢、储运到应用，包头的“风、光、氢、储、车”产业链正加速贯通。
产业加速成势，离不开营商环境的有力支撑。“绿氢相比灰氢经济性不足，我们通过新能源指标让发电收益补贴制氢，也就是‘以电补氢’。”市发展改革委相关负责人介绍，2025年至2027年包头市绿氢制氢项目可享受40%上网电量指标，2027年后可享受20%上网电量指标，通过发电收益补贴制氢成本，增强企业投资布局的信心。
凭借全链条布局，包头先后获评国家能源领域氢能全链条发展区域试点、国家氢能综合应用试点。“下一步，关键是把用氢规模做大、把应用场景拓开。”市发展改革委相关负责人表示，接下来包头市将重点面向交通、天然气掺烧、化工、冶金等领域开拓绿氢应用市场，支持企业做大用氢规模，通过规模化摊薄绿氢生产成本，同时依托全国层面技术进步进一步降低制氢成本。“我们将以国家氢能区域试点和综合应用试点建设为抓手，推进氢能项目落地、完善输氢管网、拓展应用场景，全力打造全国首座全场景绿氢自循环创新城市，形成可复制推广的氢能发展‘包头模式’。”市发展改革委相关负责人说。

title: 新型碱性制氢装备亮相!阳江打造全国首个海上风电制氢项目
content:
10月16日，2026大湾区科学论坛绿能产业科技创新分论坛暨大湾区绿能大会期间，阳江市副市长刘德伟与中国科学院院士张跃一起到访宝武清能(阳江)绿氢产业创新研究院，参观科研成果展示。张跃院士团队学术骨干康卓教授具体介绍相关研发成果，聚焦波动性绿电消纳、海上风电制氢、绿氢制造装备迭代升级等议题深入交流。
张跃院士团队骨干康卓教授现场介绍相关研发成果
据悉，该研究院由张跃院士团队与宝武清洁能源有限公司(下称“宝武清能”)联合共建，深耕绿氢关键材料与装备技术攻关，为绿氢制造降本增效提供核心技术支撑。
现场展示了多项阶段性成果。其中，新型碱性制氢装备是张跃院士团队联合宝武清能取得的最新研发成果。针对绿氢产业痛点，秉持“深绿”理念，装备核心催化组件采用团队自研超低成本、超低能耗、耐波动、长寿命的非贵金属基纳米催化材料，并在绿电波动输入工况下展现出优异的服役稳定性。目前，团队已建成全球首条纳米催化组件数字孪生智能制造产线，完成了纳米催化材料从实验室基础研发到工业化规模生产的全链条技术攻关，保障绿氢能够“产得快、产得稳、用得起”。
宝武清能(阳江)绿氢产业创新研究院
“阳江海上风电制氢项目将会成为中国首个海上风电直连制氢项目。”张跃院士说，通过“绿电直连、绿氢直供”，带动绿氢制-储-运-用上下游产业集群协同发展，推动氢能“1+N+X”多场景示范应用。项目规划建设年产8万吨绿氢生产基地，是目前粤港澳大湾区最大的绿氢产业项目。
世界风电看中国，海上风电看阳江
张跃院士团队将继续积极响应国家战略导向，推动科研范式从“成果后转化”向“创新前协同”深度转变，进一步深化产学研用创新协同，立足阳江海上风电优势，与宝武清能联合推进，构建“海上风电+绿电制氢+低碳冶金”的产业新模式，填补绿电直连制氢技术在氢冶金领域的应用空白，助力阳江打造全国绿氢技术策源地和产业高地，服务广东省绿色能源产业和地方经济高质量发展。
