title: Petrovietnam strengthens offshore wind partnerships during Denmark visit
content:
Within the context of a state visit to Denmark by Vietnam’s General Secretary
and President To Lam, Petrovietnam advanced agreements with Danish partners,
including Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP).
The agreement relates to the Nam Trung Bo 1 offshore wind project and follows
a joint development agreement signed by the companies in August 2025.
The project remains in the early stages of development. However, according
to a previous announcement from CIP, the offshore wind farm is expected
to support Vietnam’s green energy transition while creating long-term
economic value.
In addition, PTSC Marine Mechanical Services Co., Ltd. (PTSC M&C) and
Semco Maritime A/S have agreed to strengthen their strategic cooperation
between 2026 and 2030 in the offshore wind substation sector.
The partnership aims to support the development of offshore wind infrastructure
and expand international supply chain opportunities.

title: Archer pauses shareholder distributions amid wind project disputes
content:
Archer has reported third quarter EBITDA of $44.2 million, despite ongoing
commercial disputes related to the Culzean
EPC wind project.
According to the announcement the disputes remain unresolved even though
the project's main deliveries have been completed.
The company said negotiations with the client over material variation orders,
as well as a claim against a subcontractor, have taken longer than anticipated.
Archer added that the timing and value of any potential recoveries remain
uncertain.
As a result, Archer has temporarily paused shareholder distributions and
said it expects to revisit the programme in early 2027 as leverage levels
decline and visibility around the outstanding matters improves.
Archer also said it will not pursue further offshore wind EPC projects
and will instead evaluate strategic options for Archer Wind, including
a partial or full divestment.
The TotalEnergies Culzean project is located in the UK, with 3 MW expected
capacity.

title: Nexans wins key role in Mallorca-Menorca interconnection project
content:
Red Eléctrica has selected Nexans as the preferred supplier for the strategic
Mallorca-Menorca 3 interconnection project.
Under the agreement, Nexans will support Red Eléctrica, Spain’s electricity
transmission system operator, with the development of the project. The
company will also provide engineering services for a comprehensive cable
system incorporating both subsea and onshore infrastructure.
“The Mallorca-Menorca interconnection is an important infrastructure investment
that will help reinforce network resilience and support the energy transition
in the Balearic Islands,” said Pascal Radue, executive vice president
of PWR-Transmission at Nexans.
According to the company, the agreement marks the start of the engineering
phase for a new 132 kV HVAC cable link between Mallorca and Menorca. The
project is expected to strengthen the connection between the two islands
and enhance the long-term reliability of the regional power system.
Nexans said environmental stewardship will remain a key focus throughout
both the planning and execution phases of the project, reflecting the ecological
sensitivity of the area.

title: VC Firms Tap LP Pools, Warehouse Loans for Speedy AI Cash
content: When Reflection AI set out to raise $2.5 billion early this year, one of its existing venture backers, B Capital, was eager to invest again in the startup, which has emerged as the most high-profile U.S. maker of open-source AI models. But Reflection’s valuation had more than tripled in just six months, forcing investors to write big checks for a sizable stake. Such a check would have been too big for B Capital’s main venture fund, a $500 million vehicle raised in July. To come up with the cash, the company turned to a different source of capital: a pool of money apart from its regular fund, designed to give limited partners — the pension funds, endowments and wealthy individuals that back VC firms—more direct access to hot startups like Reflection at reduced fees. This strategy, known as limited partner co-investing, has become increasingly popular during the last few years as funding rounds in startups have jumped in both size and frequency. It’s just one of the ways VC firms are adapting to the immense cash demands of the AI boom. Those changes also include VC firms raising funds more frequently. They’re also taking out warehouse loans, lines of credit typically used by private equity firms. Venture capitalists are starting to tap these to come up with cash to invest in startups before the VC firms have raised money from their limited partners. For B Capital, a VC firm led by Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin and two other tech investors, the limited partner co-investment pool meant the VC firm could invest $100 million in Reflection AI—double the size of what it had previously invested in the company, according to a person with direct knowledge of the investment. VC firms have increasingly turned to such pools as startup fundraising rounds have swelled to billions of dollars at a time. The pooled limited partner funds differ from general VC funds because they tend to back just a few startups rather than the dozen-plus a more traditional fund might invest in. Limited partners have sought out these investments to get more exposure to breakout stars in venture firms’ portfolios, such as Anthropic and OpenAI. An added plus for limited partners: VC funds typically waive or reduce their fees on money raised from limited partners for these direct or co-investments. B Capital, for instance, sometimes offers co-investment opportunities with no management fee and a 10% performance fee, often known as carried interest, as opposed to the 2% management fee and 20% performance fee traditional for most VC funds, according to the person. The co-investment pools also mean there’s money ready when the startup signals it’s raising again. In the past, a VC firm could spend a few weeks negotiating one-off agreements with individual limited partners to come up with enough cash to invest in a hot startup. These days, such lengthy negotiations could cause an investment firm to lose its allocation—the right to invest in a company—say venture capitalists and limited partners. B Capital is far from the only VC firm to have pursued this strategy. Lightspeed Venture Partners brought limited partners into over $5 billion worth of co-investments over the last five years, according to a person with knowledge of its investments. Lightspeed used that money to invest in Anthropic and other startups alongside investments from its general funds. The firm typically waived management fees and reduced carried interest fees for the limited partner co-investments. Thrive Capital has invited limited partners to co-invest while it has led huge funding rounds into companies including OpenAI . For instance, CalPERS—the California pension fund giant—invested in a Thrive special purpose vehicle that raised over $744 million to invest in Stripe in 2023. VC firms are coming up with creative solutions to keep up with the steep cash needs of AI startups. Startup fundraises of over $100 million made up over 87% of all the money invested by VC firms in the first half of the year, according to data firm PitchBook. To meet their needs, some of the largest VC firms, including Thrive Capital, General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz , have in the past year raised new funds less than two years after their last fundraising, bucking the typical two- to three-year cadence typical of most VC funds. Megafunds are “constantly out there keeping checkwriters warm in advance of quickly raising a new fund,” said Peter Werner, chair of law firm Cooley’s global business department. Warehouse Loans VC firms are also beginning to explore other tactics that have been more popular with other types of investment firms, such as PE and real estate managers. JP Morgan Chase is among the banks working with VC firms to make warehouse loans, a short- to medium-term revolving line of credit that can help the firms invest before they’ve secured the capital to do so, according to someone familiar with the bank’s thinking. Warehouse loans also let the borrower take on some leverage, which can boost investment returns by minimizing the initial cash the firms must put forward to close investments. A handful of VC funds are also classified as registered investment advisers, a designation that makes it easier to use short-term debt because it removes restrictions on how much debt a given firm can hold. Warehouse loans are different from capital call credit lines , a type of loan VC firms have used for years. The firms draw on such credit lines after they’ve received commitments from limited partners for money but before the money has hit their account. “The need to move at lightning speed to capitalize on some of these opportunities” is driving demand for loans, said Cooley’s Werner.

title: Ramp Investors Went Nuclear Against Airwallex After Doomed Deal
content: In April 2025, Eric Glyman, co-founder and co-CEO of Ramp, received some bad news: A deal was falling apart. Glyman had been hoping Ramp, a highly valued startup that sells corporate credit cards and expense management software, could strike a partnership with Airwallex—a fast-growing fintech founded in Melbourne, Australia—that would improve Ramp’s ability to handle international payments. But now Airwallex CEO Jack Zhang was pulling the plug on the proposed deal—partly because of pressure from investors who wanted his company to compete with Ramp, according to employees of both companies. Glyman made an attempt to salvage the partnership, according to people familiar with discussions between the two companies. Zhang demurred. Soon after, Glyman warned Zhang that the relationship between their companies might not be so friendly in the future, according to people familiar with the situation. In the wake of the canceled deal, some of Ramp’s high-profile, politically connected investors have launched a public and private campaign to urge the U.S. government to saddle Airwallex with a government investigation that probes any links the company may have with the Chinese government. Those investors have alleged that the Chinese government could access customer data passing through Airwallex subsidiaries in China. The campaign against Airwallex brings into stark relief how the current geopolitical climate makes it possible for a company’s adversaries to weaponize perceived ties to China against it. The fact that the fight is happening between two startups in the unglamorous expense and money-processing businesses underscores how fierce the competition can get in what might otherwise appear to be a sleepy corner of tech. Airwallex sells a web-based platform to businesses for sending and receiving international payments. Many of the 11-year-old company’s earliest investors were Chinese firms, and during its early years, a large chunk of its staff—including many of its senior leaders—and the majority of its customers were based in China. It continues to maintain a sizable operation in mainland China, though it has never been headquartered there. One of the Ramp investors who has been working on the campaign against Airwallex is venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale, co-founder of Palantir. Lonsdale has coordinated with a political operative network partially funded by conservative activist Leonard Leo to lobby state and federal lawmakers to investigate Airwallex, according to people briefed on Lonsdale’s private remarks. Airwallex CEO and co-founder Jack Zhang. (Getty Images) That network includes State Armor Action, a think tank launched in 2024 and funded by an entity associated with Leo, according to public donor filings. State Armor, which is based in Austin, Texas, is led by Michael Lucci. Over the last year, Lucci has urged Texas lawmakers and a House of Representatives committee devoted to China to probe Airwallex in legislative hearings and through publicly released letters. Lucci was previously a senior fellow at the Cicero Institute, a think tank founded by Lonsdale. Lonsdale, Lucci and Leo did not respond to requests for comment. In addition to Lonsdale, Ramp has other high-profile investors like Founders Fund and Thrive Capital, who’ve excitedly watched the startup’s valuation soar—from $13 billion in March 2025 to $60 billion in fundraising announced this month. Its sharp-elbowed feud with Airwallex presents a real contrast to the public perception Ramp enjoys as a happy-go-lucky disruptor of a staid industry. It has reinforced that image with cutesy marketing stunts, such as its hiring of skateboarder Tony Hawk to ride a Ramp-branded half-pipe outside the New York Stock Exchange. (Glyman would not comment for this story.) Ramp co-CEO and co-founder Eric Glyman. (Getty Images) The battle comes at a key moment for Airwallex. Its valuation has risen quickly, too—from $8 billion in December 2025 to $11 billion in June this year—and it has its own collection of prominent investors, like T. Rowe Price and Baillie Gifford, a large European money management firm. To keep growing, the startup has been hoping to seize more business for itself in America, eyeing a potential IPO. In December 2025, it said it would crown another headquarters beyond its existing one in Singapore—on Spear Street in San Francisco’s Financial District. To mount a defense against the attacks, Airwallex has brought on former U.S. Attorney General Bill Barr as an adviser and lobbyist. “Global banking and payments companies operate internationally as a matter of course, with teams and operations across multiple markets. That is not in itself a basis for suspicion,” said Barr. He criticized the efforts to spark U.S. government investigations into Airwallex as “deeply inappropriate.…Our national security professionals have serious threats to contend with, and their time and resources should not be diverted by Silicon Valley rivalries.” A Deal Gone Bad Partnership discussions between Ramp and Airwallex began around 2023 when Airwallex approached Ramp for help solving a problem. Ramp’s focus on the U.S. market had left it vulnerable to competitors that have global payments licenses and other capabilities for moving money around the world. Its operation wasn’t as far-reaching, and it hoped a partnership with Airwallex would enable it to add more international customers. Ramp wanted to structure the deal so it could promise customers that none of their data would be stored in China or handled by Chinese staff. The talks fell apart when Airwallex told Ramp it wasn’t possible for international payments to be handled strictly by its U.S. operations if those customers were in China or Hong Kong—payments sent overseas would have to involve Airwallex’s subsidiaries around the world. (An Airwallex spokesperson said that staff based in China and Hong Kong can’t access U.S. customer data and such an arrangement goes beyond U.S. government requirements.) No deal was signed, and discussions between Ramp and Airwallex fell away until they resumed in 2025. As Ramp and Airwallex began talking again, some of Airwallex’s investors grew unhappy about the brewing partnership. They were eager for Airwallex to compete directly with Ramp, wary of how Ramp handled cross-border transactions and aspects of its offshore corporate credit card business, people familiar with the situation said. After Zhang pulled the plug on the partnership in April 2025, Airwallex launched an expense management and corporate card product the following month that seeks to rival Ramp’s own flagship product in the U.S. A Ramp spokesperson said that the companies were unable to agree on legal terms. Keith Rabois, a Ramp board director and investor, said he thinks Airwallex withdrew because it feared a Ramp deal would expose Airwallex’s inability to shield data from the Chinese government. “It’s unprecedented for a company to walk away from a negotiation at the last minute based upon a request for data protection assurances without proposing an alternative,” Rabois said. An Airwallex spokesperson disputed Rabois’ analysis of the events. “We walked away from a commercial relationship with Ramp in 2025 because we knew our competing products would complicate our relationship…during contract discussions, Ramp asked questions about data access and storage. We answered those questions, and Ramp was fully prepared to move forward,” said the spokesperson. “We understand this was not the outcome the Ramp team wanted, but it was the right strategic decision for Airwallex.” The ‘Oppo Smear’ The first sign of political trouble for Airwallex came in December 2025 when Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, a vocal critic of China, issued a public letter urging then–Attorney General Pam Bondi to investigate whether the Chinese Communist Party could access Airwallex data. According to a person close to the company, Zhang was caught off guard when he learned of Cotton’s efforts shortly after leaving lunch with an investor in London. Around the same time, Rabois wrote a post on X that criticized Airwallex as “a Chinese backdoor into sensitive American data.” (Rabois’ husband is U.S. Under Secretary of State Jacob Helberg, who previously campaigned to ban TikTok over its Chinese ties.) Then, a month ago, Rep. John Moolenaar, chair of the House committee on China, sent a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urging an investigation into Airwallex and published the letter publicly. Rabois and Lonsdale, a prominent Republican donor, amplified the letter online through posts on X, while another Ramp adviser and shareholder—Lulu Cheng Meservey, a widely followed public relations operative—alleged in a post on X that Airwallex was “under investigation for enabling ccp access to financial data.” (Meservey declined to elaborate on any knowledge she had of an investigation, saying in an email that she hasn’t “followed Senator Cotton’s concerns closely.”) Venture capitalist Joe Lonsdale, an investor in Ramp, has been an active force in the efforts to spark investigations into Airwallex, a Ramp rival. (Getty Images) The Treasury Department has not said whether it is investigating Airwallex. According to an Airwallex spokesperson, a recent assessment of its data handling by Coalfire, a Chicago-based cybersecurity firm, concluded that Airwallex has “robust” controls to prevent unauthorized access of customer data by employees or vendors in China and Hong Kong. One Lonsdale X post also mentioned Rippling, another valuable U.S.-based fintech that competes with Ramp. In the post , Lonsdale insinuated that Rippling might have a partnership with Airwallex—and that Rippling customers should be concerned about the Chinese government getting access to some data. In a reply to Lonsdale’s post, Rippling CEO and co-founder Parker Conrad said his company doesn’t have a relationship with Airwallex and labeled Lonsdale’s remarks against Airwallex as “an oppo smear by Ramp.” He was referring to opposition research, a tactic used in both politics and the corporate world to dig up information on a company that would present it in a bad light. Often such campaigns are rooted in a few facts and a good amount of media spin. A Rise in China Zhang’s investors and supporters see him as a rags-to-riches entrepreneur whose unrelenting work ethic has turned Airwallex into a fast-growing startup with an enviable reach through the global financial system. In the third quarter of this year, Airwallex hit $1.5 billion in annualized revenue by facilitating payments for China-based e-commerce companies and becoming an international payments platform for fast-growing startups such as Brex and Deel. Along with major U.S. and European investors, Airwallex has attracted some of the largest venture capitalists in Australia, where producing a unicorn startup has been a rarity. Several years ago, Stripe offered $1.2 billion for the company. Zhang turned down the offer. Zhang moved from Qingdao, China, to Australia in 2000 at age 15 to attend high school, living with a host family. Shortly after, his banker father, who remained in China with the rest of Zhang’s family, lost his job and couldn’t financially support Zhang anymore. When Zhang got to college, he earned money with a series of odd jobs—washing dishes, bartending and clerking at a gas station. After graduating, Zhang developed trading systems for National Australia Bank, a major financial institution in the country. He kept up side hustles exporting olive oil and wine and developing real estate that delivered him a nest egg worth about $10 million, he said in a 2025 podcast interview . In 2015, he decided to launch Airwallex while running a coffee shop in Melbourne: He’d gotten the idea for a startup that could simplify sending money across borders after he ran into difficulties buying cups and coffee beans overseas using traditional banks and payment methods. Zhang assembled a plan for Airwallex with the help of three friends he’d met at the University of Melbourne: Max Li, Ki-lok Wong and Jacob Dai, all of whom became co-founders. Li discussed the concept for Airwallex with Lucy Yueting Liu, a young former investment consultant for China International Capital Corp., a large Chinese investment bank, who invested $1 million. She became a co-founder as well and served as the company’s first chief operating officer. (Airwallex’s founders hold Australian citizenship, and Liu holds a New Zealand passport). Airwallex early backers included Chinese groups such as Hong Kong–based Gobi Zhiying and Tencent. (In 2025, the U.S. government designated Tencent a Chinese military company.) Sequoia’s former Chinese venture arm also invested. GOP Rep. John Moolenaar has urged the Treasury Department to investigate Airwallex. (Getty Images) In 2018, Shanghai-based Huashan Capital sued Airwallex, alleging that Zhang had failed to pay for shares he had bought back from the investor. The case was settled, and Huashan is no longer an investor. That same year, Airwallex, which Zhang incorporated in the Cayman Islands, moved its headquarters from Melbourne to Hong Kong, in part to apply for a banking license. Its main customers at the time were in China and Southeast Asia, and they included JD.com , the Chinese e-commerce giant. Often Airwallex would fly new employees hired in the U.S. to its offices in China to meet senior executives. As the company grew, workers based in China sometimes clashed with the Western employees, who had a more laid-back approach, said several former employees. Staff dedicated to financial crimes compliance who were based outside China sometimes argued with Airwallex’s China-based sales employees about how to handle financial and legal risks, those former employees said. Soon, Airwallex focused on expanding outside of China. In 2023, the company moved its headquarters to Singapore. Its series of recent fundraisings has shifted the makeup of its cap table and diminished the prominence of its early Chinese investors. Tencent now holds less than 10% of the company and has no access to information beyond those of any other minority shareholder, according to Airwallex. About a quarter of the company’s staff is now based in China, and a third of the company’s revenue now comes from Europe and the U.S. Last January, the company faced a round of negative press in Australia after the country’s anti–money-laundering regulator ordered an audit of Airwallex’s financial crime controls. That bad press came just after Airwallex had sent legal letters to several Australia publications, hoping to get those outlets to remove stories they had published about its workplace and its handling of financial crime controls, including some stories from years earlier, according to people familiar with the matter. Allies in America To respond to the assault in the U.S. by Ramp’s investors, Airwallex has called in the cavalry. Barr, the former U.S. attorney general for Presidents George H.W. Bush and Donald Trump, recently lobbied the Department of Justice on behalf of Airwallex, according to lobbying disclosures. The company’s representatives met with Senator Cotton’s staff in July to assuage his concerns and met with other members of the executive branch and in Congress, according to people briefed on the meetings. And to combat what it sees as unfair media coverage, the company has enlisted law firm Clare Locke, now known for handling legal matters for prominent people and companies in the Trump orbit, according to people familiar with the matter. To further build a presence in America, Airwallex is now an advertising sponsor of “All-In,” the podcast hosted by venture capitalists Chamath Palihapitiya, David Sacks, David Friedberg and Jason Calacanis. And during the latest season of Major League Baseball, Airwallex became the official jersey patch sponsor for the San Francisco Giants baseball team, replacing the logo of a venerable American icon: Chevrolet.

title: Anthropic’s Elevator Problem: Persuading Investors to Share Its AI Dream
content: One quotation has rattled around in my head for a while, which I first heard from early Anthropic investor Jaan Tallinn: “The future of the world will be decided by a group of people who fit in an elevator.” The enigmatic billionaire said on a podcast earlier this year that a friend had used the illustration to describe the concentration of power at the leading AI companies. I’ve been reflecting on it as Anthropic prepares for its Wall Street debut because the company’s small group of powerful insiders, who are set to realize incredible wealth at unprecedented speed, face their biggest test in explaining themselves to the world outside their elevator. To raise the money Anthropic leaders need, and to keep raising it again and again, big fund managers need to fully buy in. This is the stark divide worth watching as Anthropic’s IPO gets closer, with a prospectus likely to drop in the coming days en route to a listing expected next month. Anthropic employees and executives, closest to the action and with the most to gain, have deep faith about the power of AI and its ability to take over all kinds of work and make scientific breakthroughs that will power the company’s success for years to come. For instance, the company published in a little-noticed report last week, titled “ AI Expectations Gap ,” that 91% of the 1,300 Anthropic employees surveyed believed AI would be able to make a Nobel Prize-level breakthrough by 2030, compared to 39% of Americans surveyed. Another report released the same day about how Anthropic’s own jobs are changing said hours worked by AI agents inside the company outnumbered human employees six to one. Wall Street, meanwhile, doesn’t have the same conviction about the future of the AI industry that it will need to keep funding. You see the anxiety and gyrations around AI cloud companies, semiconductor firms and cybersecurity stocks. You also see it in the reaction to Anthropic's meeting last week with potential investors , some of whom came away thinking that its rapid growth isn't enough to justify the IPO valuation of nearly $2 trillion that some bankers have floated privately. As things stand, Anthropic would be going public as Wall Street confidence on AI is the lowest it has been all year. Even numbers-oriented corporate finance executives at the big companies most likely to tout the benefits of AI—the big banks getting paid big fees to take Anthropic and other AI giants public—still stop short of laying out the hard-and-fast financial upside of the technology. “The benefits aren't observable in our current quarterly earnings,” JPMorgan finance chief Jeremy Barnum said on an analyst call last week, before clarifying his personal excitement about the technology’s potential. “So how long is it going to take for that to show up? We'll see. And obviously, some of those benefits are going to be offset by token costs, which is a whole other conversation,” Barnum added. These are the conversations Amodei and other Anthropic executives will need to have in the coming weeks, as they have to convince investors they have can tackle their most obvious challenge: increasing competition from open-source AI models that do a lot of white-collar work well enough for a fraction of the price Anthropic charges. The company, despite its jaw-dropping growth, still faces doubts that it will ever achieve the kind of business dominance that investors truly salivate over. Peter Thiel, the tech investor who once wrote that “competition is for losers,” said on Walter Isaacson’s podcast this week that the AI business remains a heated race. “It’s the furthest thing from a monopoly imaginable,” he said. He added that while Anthropic had grabbed the lead from OpenAI, “it also still feels that Google and Meta and Grok are not that far behind. I'm not sure China is that far behind.” That leaves some big future questions hanging over this IPO: Will Anthropic lose its lead? And if it does, how will the company respond? How will Wall Street? I spoke to several current and former employees, as well as Anthropic executives, while profiling Amodei over the summer . The company’s most unusual trait—and potential blind spot—is its quasi-religious faith in Amodei to guide all of them into the singularity, or the time when AI exceeds human capabilities. His power appears to come from not only creating a culture of free-flowing candor, but also a track record of accurate predictions. Right now, Anthropic, and Amodei himself, seem to vibrate with confidence. Big money managers who attended the investor day in San Francisco last week called his presentation “uplifting.” In the coming weeks, that confident performance could very well help assuage a wary Wall Street. Or Amodei could take for granted that investors aren’t nearly as certain about the near-term economic power of AI as he is—or as anyone who fits inside Anthropic’s elevator every day. title: Why Blackstone Thinks AI Bottlenecks Could Work in its Favor
content: Greetings! On their earnings calls earlier in the week, Meta Platforms and SpaceX delivered the same underlying message to investors: demand for AI is running ahead of the supply of AI compute. On Thursday, another important player in the AI ecosystem—Blackstone, the alternative asset management giant—repeated a version of that refrain. On its own earnings call, the firm, a major investor at the center of the AI data center boom, faced pointed questions from analysts about rising financing costs and mounting investor concerns over the sustainability of the buildout. Its executives argued that the very factors threatening the AI industry’s expansion could actually work in Blackstone’s favor. CEO Steve Schwarzman noted that constraints on power availability and growing public opposition to new data centers are making it harder to bring new capacity online, potentially making existing facilities more valuable. Blackstone President Jon Gray also suggested the firm could seek higher returns on projects where it hasn’t signed leases yet in order to offset rising borrowing costs. Blackstone’s third-quarter results offered some support for that argument: Its infrastructure investments were buoyed by what executives called “extraordinary” data center leasing momentum, significantly outperforming its broader private equity and real estate holdings. “Despite all the negative things you’re reading about AI today, when we look across our business, this continues to be the area where we’re driving the highest returns,” Gray said during the call. But it’s hard to ignore the fact that the financing concerns and roadblocks threatening the broader AI infrastructure buildout are also hitting closer to home for Blackstone. Fears about rising financing costs have sent CoreWeave’s stock and bond prices plunging—the neocloud’s shares closed down another 10% Thursday after sliding last week—while Australian AI cloud provider Firmus abruptly pulled its initial public offering earlier this month. Blackstone has provided billions in loans to CoreWeave and has both invested in and lent money to Firmus. Blackstone has also been pressing ahead with brand-new AI ventures. In May, the firm announced an initial $5 billion equity commitment to a joint venture with Google to create a new cloud company that will use Google’s TPU chips, with plans to bring 500 megawatts of capacity online by next year. The venture could need as much as $25 billion in total investment, including some borrowed money, and it has reportedly encountered delays at potential data center sites. Blackstone, for its part, says that broader anxiety about AI hasn’t undermined its ability to raise fresh cash for making its own investments. “We’re continuing to be able to raise capital. Obviously investors are asking the same question around AI, but what we continue to see is demand and usage of the AI going up faster than the compute,” Gray said. While Blackstone says it wants to continue going big in AI, it can only finance a tiny portion of the industry’s broader infrastructure buildout itself. The trillions of dollars of financing needed for chips and data centers in the coming years requires raising money from a far broader pool of investors. Blackstone itself has said it’s not clear where all the money will come from. Jas Khaira, the head of the team leading Blackstone’s push into AI investment, said late last month that the firm is still trying to determine which investors across the public debt and private credit markets will be able to provide the funding needed to sustain the buildout. “We have not mapped out who’s going to buy all the debt. We have some hypotheses, but the honest answer is we don’t know where all of it will come from,” he said at The Information’s AI Agenda event in San Francisco. Data Center Headwinds Despite Blackstone’s overall positive note on AI demand, we got fresh evidence Thursday afternoon of the uncertainty in the IPO market for companies in the data center business. Phoebe Liu and Valida Pau had a scoop that SB Energy, a company controlled by SoftBank Group that is developing an OpenAI data center in Ohio, is discussing a plan to put off its IPO until December or earlier next year. Previously, SB Energy was aiming to go public in September. The best hope for an SB Energy IPO is that the supply of AI compute gets so tight that investors start warming back up to data centers. —Nick Wingfield In Other News Meta Platforms’ stock fell 7% as investor enthusiasm over its third-quarter earnings report on Wednesday gave way to concerns about the probability that it will need to issue new equity to pay for its AI spending. Andreessen Horowitz renamed its flagship blockchain fund a16z Frontier, dropping “crypto” from its name (The Information’s earlier scoop on the change is here ). Google partnered with energy company Voltus to pay homes and businesses to use less electricity during periods of peak demand. title: Salesforce Customers Brace For New Fees to Use Claude in Its Apps
content: Salesforce is leading the software industry’s attempt to collect fees from businesses that use Claude and other external AI tools to automate work in enterprise apps. As soon as next month, Salesforce plans to require companies to register outside AI agents, a step toward charging them each time those agents update or analyze data stored in Salesforce. The fees let Salesforce earn money from customers who use such AI instead of paying for Salesforce’s built-in AI products. The Salesforce tollgate has implications for the rest of the industry, which is coming to terms with the idea that so-called AI agents may be able to use software firms’ apps more efficiently than humans do, meaning their seat-based or per-user pricing model might not have staying power. The question is whether the new AI tollgates—which Atlassian, Workday, ServiceNow and Datadog are also erecting to various extents—and other pricing shifts will more than make up for an eventual decline in per-seat subscription revenues. The vast majority of workers haven’t yet outsourced such work to AI, of course, and companies like Salesforce are trying to get more revenue from them as well. They charge fees based on how much they use the apps’ built-in AI tools and are also experimenting with outcome-based pricing, meaning customers only pay when such tools actually complete a task successfully or help the customers make more money. For now, Salesforce and some other software firms developing tollgates for customers’ AI agents haven’t started charging the tolls. They’re letting customers experiment for free with the technology a little while longer. (The customers still have to pay providers such as Anthropic to use the AI agents in the first place.) Starting around November, according to the company’s website , Salesforce will require customers to register any externally-made AI agents if they plan to use them to take actions on their behalf in Salesforce apps. Each action an agent takes in Salesforce counts as a billable “interaction,” according to the company. The move has lifted investor confidence in Salesforce recently. Salesforce describes the registration requirement as a security measure because the company gives each agent its own identity and narrower data-access permissions, compared to humans. It isn’t clear how Salesforce will clamp down on customers using their own AI agents, such as OpenClaw-powered ones that run on a person’s computer and can access any app that runs on it. (Salesforce did not respond to requests for comment.) Salesforce hasn’t announced prices tied to such agent usage, but customers could eventually end up paying a lot more money than they do now, given how many of them are already using their own AI on top of Salesforce apps and bypassing Salesforce’s own built-in AI tools, according to software consultants and chief information officers. Nick Hamm, a software consultant, said that most of the 150 enterprises he works with are currently using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to automate work inside Salesforce apps, for free. But they’re reconsidering that usage in anticipation of the upcoming fees. If the fees are too high, the customers may move their business data outside of Salesforce’s apps so they can use AI to analyze the data without paying an extra cost, he said. New customers will have a three month grace period after the new pricing is announced to register their AI agents, and the pricing won’t affect existing customers until their contracts are renewed. In addition to the billable “interactions,” customers have the option to buy unlimited agent usage by purchasing a “headless license,” a Salesforce account executive told Hamm in a LinkedIn message viewed by The Information. Some customers such as Lumen, a fiber-optic network provider to enterprises and data centers, say they are waiting to test Salesforce’s new connectors until pricing is disclosed. So far, Lumen has leaned on Salesforce’s built-in AI. A longtime customer of Salesforce’s customer relationship management software, Lumen made a “major” investment in using Salesforce’s AI sales agents in the last 12 months, according to CIO Jim Fowler. The sales agents help with tasks such as collecting customer information and generating sales quotes for the customers to buy fiber connections between data centers, saving Lumen’s human salespeople considerable time, he said. So far, Fowler said, Salesforce has been “super flexible” about letting Lumen use existing subscription fees to also cover its use of built-in AI features such as the sales agents. Early customer reactions to the pricing announcement will likely determine how flexible Salesforce is with customers that start renewing their contracts after November. If its past AI pricing efforts are any guide, Salesforce could easily switch things up depending on the feedback, or any blowback, it receives. title: SB Energy Considers Waiting Until December or Later for an IPO
content: SB Energy, the SoftBank Group–controlled developer of a massive planned Ohio data center project for OpenAI, is considering going public in December or possibly waiting until next year, according to people familiar with the discussions. That is a later timeline than previously expected. The data center developer was aiming to go public as soon as September, The Information reported in August . But since then, the public market has soured on initial public offerings from data center and AI cloud companies. Australian cloud firm Firmus yanked its IPO plans earlier this month, and others are considering delaying their offerings. SB Energy leaders are closely watching Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO, which is expected next month before the Thanksgiving holiday, said the people. SB Energy could try to go public as soon as December if Anthropic’s public listing trades well. SB Energy made its IPO prospectus public on September 2 and filed an amended one on September 21. Companies usually start their formal marketing with IPO investors, known as an IPO road show, two weeks after they file publicly with the Securities and Exchange Commission, though they can choose to wait longer—particularly when markets are volatile or unpredictable. The company’s IPO is one of several expected offerings aiming to tap public investors’ cash to feed the physical expansion necessary to run and train AI. SB Energy had been aiming to raise $5 billion to $7 billion to help finance the Ohio data center that OpenAI plans to lease. The data center is set to be backed with a $105 billion credit guarantee from Nvidia and to use Nvidia chips. If it puts off its IPO for longer, SB Energy could continue to expand using the cash it’s already raised. That’s thanks in part to a $1.5 billion investment in SB Energy by Nvidia in mid-August when the two companies and OpenAI signed the data center deal. In addition, SB Energy had $1.2 billion of cash and cash equivalents as of June 30. SB Energy could also tap private investors, including two of its shareholders, SoftBank and Nvidia, which are already big backers. That’s a path Firmus, which is in talks to raise hundreds of millions of dollars from Nvidia in a private round , is also pursuing. Still, going public would make it easier for SB Energy to raise the more than $100 billion it needs to achieve its ambitious plans to build a data center in Ohio that could generate 8.5 gigawatts of compute and hold some $600 billion in Nvidia hardware. The public offering would pave the wave for cheaper debt sales to finance that project. A representative for SB Energy declined to comment. Valuation Concerns SB Energy’s revenue is now largely dependent on the sale of electricity to power companies. Its eventual public offering will rely on investor confidence that its plans to expand its revenue will come to fruition. Bankers have floated a valuation around $60 billion, but IPO investors have found that hard to stomach, The Information reported last month . That’s because SB Energy is asking investors for a valuation based mostly on future revenue that depends on whether its massive data center projects get built. The Ohio data center constitutes most of the firm’s $430 billion in contracted data center revenue. SB Energy aims to have the facility come online in phases, beginning in 2028, and the revenue would be spread over 15 year to 20 year lease terms starting when each building comes online. The company reported $139 million in revenue in the first half of 2026; based on an annualized version of that figure, a $60 billion valuation would amount to a revenue multiple of more than 200. SB Energy is weighing its IPO timing as a slew of data center developers are also aiming to go public soon in the U.S. Nscale, which develops data centers and rents out Nvidia’s AI chips, is trying to stick with a planned fall listing at a valuation of around $30 billion, even after some prospective investors voiced skepticism about the valuation, said people familiar with the matter. It’s in talks with Anthropic about a cloud computing deal worth $45 billion, which could help support that valuation, said one of the people. Some of those other developers are reconsidering their options after yields on some CoreWeave bonds , which have become a proxy for investors’ perception of the AI boom’s risks, spiked and share prices of publicly traded neoclouds sank over the past weeks. DayOne Data Centers, a Singapore-based data center operator, is now weighing whether it should push back its offering or raise less money in the IPO, according to Bloomberg. ( DayOne is the developer for one of Firmus’ biggest sites in Indonesia, a facility that’s set to be filled with more than 170,000 of Nvidia’s most advanced AI server chips.) Blackstone-backed data center operator AirTrunk recently postponed the listing of a real estate investment trust on the Singapore Exchange that sought to raise about $1.5 billion.

title: Datadog Offered $4 Billion to Buy Cloud Security Startup ‘Upwind’
content: Enterprise software firm Datadog recently offered to buy Israeli cloud cybersecurity startup Upwind Security for nearly $4 billion, according to someone with direct knowledge of the talks, the latest sign of white-hot interest in such firms. Upwind has fielded other takeover attempts from multiple bidders in recent months but hasn’t accepted any offers. It is finalizing a $300 million funding round at a roughly $3.8 billion valuation, meaning the Datadog offer doesn’t carry much of a premium over the private valuation, said two people with knowledge of the situation. The startup sells software to keep tabs on applications, including so-called AI agents, that run in the cloud and to detect and automatically respond to potential evidence of hacks or breaches. Datadog, which has a $90 billion market capitalization, sells so-called data observability software that helps companies collect and observe data from a wide range of software applications. It also sells security software, meaning adding real-time security capabilities from a product like Upwind’s could be a fit. The deal discussions come as the cybersecurity sector has been rocked by AI-related threats, as new AI models have shown they can find serious flaws in widely used software, such as the code underlying the PHP programming language, that attackers could exploit. Companies are planning to spend a lot more on cybersecurity software in the wake of such threats. More businesses are using AI agents that connect to other cloud-hosted applications within their systems for tasks like generating and running applications or automating workplace tasks. That has sparked demand for software to track the agents, such as Upwind’s, according to executives who buy security software. Companies such as Roku and Brazilian neobank Nubank use Upwind’s software to monitor and protect their cloud-hosted applications, according to Upwind’s website. Datadog tried to buy Upwind last year for around $1 billion, one of the people said, but the talks petered out at the time. Upwind has since grown quickly: its annual recurring revenue has exceeded $50 million, implying about $4 million in revenue per month, up from roughly $20 million in ARR at the end of 2025, according to someone with knowledge of the figures . A deal at close to $4 billion would be around 80 times the startup’s ARR, which is higher than the revenue multiple of Google’s takeover of cloud security firm Wiz earlier this year. A representative of Upwind did not have a comment, and Datadog did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Large security software providers Palo Alto Networks, Google, and Crowdstrike have each acquired cloud security startups that compete in some areas with Upwind in recent years, including Google’s $32 billion acquisition of Wiz. Upwind, founded in 2022 by CEO Amiram Shachar, has already raised over $400 million in total, including a $250 million round in January that valued it at $1.5 billion. Its biggest backers include Bessemer Venture Partners, Craft Ventures, and Cyberstarts; other investors include Salesforce Ventures and Greylock. Globes and Bloomberg earlier reported on the startup’s ongoing funding round.

title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
content:
The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots
Plus: Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises
Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on. Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely. Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please. Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really?
In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades. From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come.
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up.
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download. So stay tuned!
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
—Jessica Hamzelou
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. This is why it left me questioning how we cover science.
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.
Help choose our next Roundtables topic
Our subscriber-only Roundtables bring you into conversation with MIT Technology Review editors and reporters. Now, we want your help choosing our next topic: how to keep your mind going for longer, or what it would take to put a city on the moon. Which do you most want to hear about?
Vote for your preferred topic by Monday at 12 p.m. ET.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Palmer Luckey’s new startup plans to genetically enhance military dogs
Warhound says the dogs will detect explosives and protect troops. (Wired $)
+ It’s raised $200 million from investors, including Sequoia. (TechCrunch)
+ Colossal Biosciences will help clone and gene-edit the dogs. (Bloomberg $)
+ The Pentagon wants an AI-powered lie detector. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Donald Trump says Elon Musk has restored Ukraine’s Starlink access
But Zelensky says Starlink speeds remained capped. (Reuters $)
+ Trump reportedly asked Musk to lift the speed limits. (WSJ $)
3 The newly disclosed PHP flaw is yet to yield successful attacks
Experts say the vulnerabilities are harder to exploit than expected. (NBC News)
+ Officials urged patches after the flaws forced websites offline worldwide. (BBC)
+ But publicly disclosed fixes can help hackers. (The Economist $)
4 Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death by 42%
The vaccine reduced melanoma patients’ risk of recurrence. (Ars Technica)
+ Federal health agencies are abandoning mRNA. (MIT Technology Review)
5 A powerful new gene editor has reached its first human patient
The prime editing technique rewrites DNA in liver cells. (Nature)
+ Companies are planning gene-edited babies. (MIT Technology Review)
6 Google will pay customers to free up power for data centers
Its virtual power plant will reward people for adjusting energy usage. (NYT $)
+ It’s also illegally felled 250,000 trees in Finland for a data center. (Guardian)
7 Dutch spies reportedly hacked Jared Kushner’s iPhone
The report alleges financial links to foreign officials. (Vanity Fair $)
8 Fossil fuels may have stopped the next ice age
Modern warming reversed 2,000 years of ice growth. (Wired $)
9 Scientists have recreated solar flares to explain the corona’s mystery
They hope to explain why it’s so hot. (New Scientist $)
10 A road trip with America’s cheapest EV shows charging is much improved
Fast chargers kept the journey manageable despite sparse coverage. (WSJ $)
+ And bigger EVs aren’t always better. (MIT Technology Review)
Quote of the day
“If anything happens to this guy, that's just it. Everyone is screwed.”
—Software developer Ian Landsman says on X that volunteer Ondřej Surý’s work on patching PHP vulnerabilities makes him an unsung hero of the entire internet.
One more thing
How sounds can turn us on to the wonders of the universe
For decades, astronomy has relied on visual information to make sense of the cosmos: images, charts, and graphs. Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe.
Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed. The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education.
Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing.
—Corey S. Powell
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
content:
In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
A reporter’s unsettling takeaway from You Can See Everything.
Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything, the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.
I went in not really knowing what to expect. I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!). I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood, and the Hulu series The Dropout, starring Amanda Seyfried.
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled. But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects. The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything.
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19. She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood.
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014. Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old.
Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work. Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead. MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015.
Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016. That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong.
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors. She began serving her sentence in May 2023.
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children. I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film.
As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer, there are plenty of super close-ups. I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people. And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out. Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind. Will anyone believe her?
I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence. And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator. You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind. At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat. Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie?
But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015. Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022.
I didn’t cover Theranos in the 2010s. If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all?
One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data. Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification. Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process. You should be able to trust published scientific papers.
Except that sometimes you can’t.
Scientists aren’t perfect. Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance. Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis. Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always. There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence. Many papers ultimately end up with corrections. Some are withdrawn—10,000 research papers were retracted in 2023.
At any rate, there’s been a shift to sharing research in other ways. Today, many scientists opt to publish their work at preprint servers like arXiv, medRxiv, and bioRxiv before they submit them to established journals. Those outlets bypass peer review. So do company press releases, social media posts, and many conference presentations. And I get a lot of my stories from conversations and interviews.
I’ll admit I’ve looked at a scientific finding and thought: A scientist has just said they’ve done that. How can I be sure they really have?
I like to think that I hold myself to high journalistic standards here, as does everyone at MIT Technology Review. I would never publish a story about some new scientific development without doing my own form of peer review, and asking scientists—ideally people I know and trust—what they think of a new claim.
But the film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative. While most scientists are, I hope, pretty honest, and Holmes is certainly an outlier, we should all continue to interrogate the claims being fed to us. If you’ve seen the film, let me know what you think!

title: Australia’s 2.2 GW Snowy 2.0 pumped hydro cost estimate rises again - Energy Storage
content: Australia’s 2.2 GW/350 GWh Snowy 2.0 pumped-storage hydroelectricity project is now expected to cost between AUD 22.5 billion and AUD 25 billion through to commissioning in 2029, according to an updated cost and schedule estimate from principal contractor Future Generation Joint Venture (FGJV). The project was initially estimated to cost AUD 2 billion when announced in early 2017. That figure was revised to AUD 3.8 billion to AUD 4.5 billion later that year, AUD 6.1 billion in 2018 and AUD 12 billion in 2023. The update attributes the cost increase largely to FGJV’s underestimation of the delivery scope, including cost and planning underperformance, and the contractor’s failure to meet productivity targets because of construction complexities. It also cites a design revamp involving detailed technical analysis, and external factors such as global cost increases for equipment, services and labor that exceeded the allowances made at a 2023 contract reset. Snowy Hydro CEO Dennis Barnes said the cost increase is disappointing, but that because the project is no longer on a fixed-price contract, it is no longer exposed to the “weight of billions of dollars in claims from the contractor.” The 2023 contract reset included mechanisms to support FGJV’s cost and program management on the project, which has more than 5,000 workers. These included directing FGJV to set up a project control office, now operational, that uses enhanced data and analytics to drive productivity and identify emerging risks early. “Like the original Snowy Scheme, which still underpins energy reliability more than 70 years on, Snowy 2.0 is a generational investment in our energy sovereignty and a national asset owned by all Australians,” Barnes said. “Snowy 2.0’s massive, long-duration storage will be the grid’s insurance policy against multi-day wind and solar droughts, helping to prevent blackouts and control price spikes that would otherwise flow through to household electricity bills.” Snowy 2.0, regarded as Australia’s largest energy security project, will provide long-duration energy storage equivalent to approximately 26 million home batteries, or enough to power 3 million homes for a week, according to Snowy Hydro. The project is transitioning from cavern excavation and machine tunneling , which are 90% and 65% complete, respectively, to the physical assembly of the large-scale underground power station . All six reversible turbines have arrived in Australia. They were manufactured by Germany-based Voith Hydro, with bespoke components fabricated at its facility in Shanghai. The underground powerhouse complex is a network of caverns about 1 km below ground, which Snowy Hydro said is comparable in scale to the Sydney Opera House. It estimates the complex will last 150 years, until 2176. In the next phase, crews will install inlet valves, spiral casings, high-voltage transformers weighing more than 400 metric tons each and other hydropower components. title: Tin-modified nanotube gel reduces solar cell temperature by 9.5 C - pv magazine Global
content:
Researchers in India have developed a reusable, thermally conductive gel that can passively cool silicon solar cells and improve their power conversion efficiency. The research aimed to develop a cost-effective and sustainable cooling solution that reduces operating temperatures, improves electrical performance, and extends the lifespan of photovoltaic devices without requiring external energy. The gel consists of polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) blended with tin (Sn)-coated and Sn-filled carbon nanotubes (Sn-CNTs).
“In the present study, Sn was employed as a coating material because of its excellent wettability, relatively low melting temperature (232 C), and good compatibility with carbon nano materials, enabling uniform coating of CNT surfaces,” the researchers explained. “Sn provides a practical balance of thermal performance, processability, interfacial compatibility, and economic feasibility, making it well-suited for enhancing the effective thermal conductivity of CNTs.”
To prepare the gel, the researchers dissolved 0.5 g of PVA in 5 ml of dimethyl sulfoxide at 120 C and added Sn-CNTs at concentrations of 0.5 wt%, 0.7 wt%, and 1.4 wt%. They stirred the mixtures for one hour and ultrasonicated them for 30 minutes before cooling and casting them into 5 cm × 5 cm molds. The samples were then kept at 0 C for 24 hours as part of a freeze-thaw crosslinking process. The team also prepared a pure PVA gel for comparison.
The scientists analyzed the gels’ structure and composition and measured their thermal conductivity, tensile strength, and thermal stability. For the cooling tests, they attached the 0.7 wt% and 1.4 wt% formulations to the rear of a commercial polycrystalline silicon solar cell and compared their performance with that of a device cooled with pure PVA gel and an uncooled reference device. They also monitored weight loss and device performance over 40 days. To assess reusability, they soaked the used 0.7 wt% gel in deionized water for 24 hours before testing it again.
“The intrinsic thermal conductivity of Sn-CNTs provides excellent heat transfer capability through the gel medium,” the researchers said. “Furthermore, PVA/Sn-CNT conducting gel manifested superior thermal conductivity of 3.2 W/mK and mechanical strength of 0.21 kPa. Consequently, the developed conducting gel highlights excellent potential for thermal management of solar cells without compromising the power conversion efficiency (PCE).”
The tests showed that the 0.7 wt% formulation reduced the solar cell’s operating temperature by 9.5 C and increased its power conversion efficiency from 12.5% to 13.2% under simulated sunlight. After 40 days, the gel-cooled device retained an efficiency of 12%, which increased to 13.3% after the gel was soaked in water and reused.
“Overall, this method offers a green, affordable pathway to boost solar efficiency, lifetime, and thermal control using sustainable materials,” the researchers concluded. However, the they did not provide a detailed cost assessment of the proposed cooling solution or compare its economic feasibility with that of existing solar cell cooling technologies.
The findings are presented in “
Reusable thermally conductive Sn-CNTs infused PVA gel for efficient silicon solar cell module cooling
,” published in
Solar Energy
. The research team included scientists from the
Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Mandi
Amity University
in India.

title: Strengthening El Niño splits South America's September solar exposure - pv magazine Global
content:
Across South America as a whole, September irradiance was close to normal, but the total average hides a sharply divided month, according to analysis using the
Solcast API
. Persistent cloud and exceptional rainfall pushed global horizontal irradiance (GHI) 20–24% below the 2007–2025 normal across southeastern Brazil. The Patagonian Steppe and Tierra del Fuego ran close to 19% below normal, while most of the north of the continent was sunnier than usual. A rapidly strengthening El Niño was an important large-scale influence, reshaping rainfall, drought and cloud patterns from the Amazon Basin to Patagonia.
The Brazilian irradiance deficit was centred on São Paulo state, extending to Rio de Janeiro, coinciding with unusually wet conditions. Rio de Janeiro recorded its wettest September since records began in 1997, with heavy rain, thunderstorms and hail across the region. Rainfall means cloud, directly suppressing irradiance. The pattern is consistent with enhanced cloud banding from the South Atlantic Convergence Zone, a band of cloud and rain that stretches from the Amazon towards the Atlantic. Regional climate assessments had identified southern and southeastern Brazil as a primary wet anomaly under El Niño. The southeast also holds Brazil’s largest concentration of utility-scale and distributed solar assets, so this will have had an outsized impact on generation.
NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center continues to issue a “El Niño Advisory” status since June, and forecasts an 80% chance of a strong-to-very-strong event persisting into early 2027. The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) named South America as one of the regions most likely to see major rainfall shifts between September and November. Above normal rainfall was expected across southern Brazil, while drought and extreme heat risks were rising across the Amazon, Colombia and northern South America.
2015 is the only year in recent history with a September super El Niño. In comparison, 2026 shows similar broad patterns, notably sunnier north, but significant local differences . A small area near Ecuador recorded GHI around 20% above normal. El Niño usually brings more cloud to the eastern tropical Pacific although these effects are typically found in the first part of the year. This is a reminder that while El Niño is a significant climate driver it isn’t the only one and what we observe is a combination of atmospheric drivers. Conditions we see maybe associated with El Niño or La Nina but direct attribution can not be made with certainty.
An area of particular contrast to 2015 was in the far south, where there was the deficit over the Patagonian Steppe and Tierra del Fuego was comparable to southern Brazil’s, thousands of kilometres away. In contrast, western Patagonia was much sunnier than usual with the Andes creating a literal and figurative divide in the south of the continent.
produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary
AI/ML algorithms
. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350GW of solar assets globally.

title: China solar module prices steady as proposed price floors meet skepticism - pv magazine Global
content:
China’s mainstream TOPCon module export prices held steady for a second week, despite efforts by major polysilicon producers to set minimum price floors on module and polysilicon products.
According to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Oct. 20, the Chinese Module Marker (CMM), the OPIS benchmark assessment for TOPCon modules below 645 W from China, was unchanged at $0.107/W Free-On-Board (FOB) China.
Forward prices were also stable, with Q1 2027 loading assessed at $0.106/W and Q2 through Q4 2027 at $0.105/W.
Under the pricing framework discussed by China’s eight major polysilicon manufacturers at an Oct. 11 meeting in Hangzhou, minimum selling prices of CNY 0.79 ($0.118) /W for TOPCon modules and CNY 0.86/W for back-contact modules were proposed, equivalent to $0.118/W and $0.129/W FOB, alongside a minimum polysilicon selling price of CNY 43/kg, inclusive of tax.
Market participants, however, remained skeptical that the proposed measures would provide price support amid persistent oversupply and weak downstream demand.
Several trade sources questioned whether the pricing discipline could be sustained, as industry self-discipline agreements do not constitute legally enforceable price controls and their effectiveness depends on manufacturers’ willingness to comply.
A source at a Chinese top-tier integrated manufacturer similarly described the proposed fixed module pricing mechanism as difficult to implement, suggesting that efforts by these major polysilicon producers to dictate downstream module prices could be “one-sided wishful thinking”.
In Oct. 2024, the China Photovoltaic Industry Association (CPIY) released an estimated photovoltaic modules production cost of CNY 0.68/W in an attempt to address below-cost bidding in large-scale procurement tenders. However, industry sources noted that the price guideline was non-binding, allowing manufacturers to continue submitting bids below the suggested floor.
Weak installation demand and pressure to clear inventories ahead of year-end could further undermine efforts to stabilize prices, sources said. A tier-1 vertically integrated manufacturer said module shipments were subdued in the third quarter, with producers likely to cut prices in the fourth quarter to stimulate sales volumes, defend market share and support revenue. The manufacturer expected prices to remain stable or edge lower through the rest of the year.
Another downstream manufacturer said the short-term price outlook would also depend on whether manufacturers could secure higher selling prices on existing inventories, adding that many producers were highly motivated to clear stocks in the final quarter of the year.
The outlook for high-efficiency modules, however, was less certain, with demand potentially strengthening in 2027 as China introduces tighter efficiency requirements and increases the adoption of higher-efficiency technologies in its domestic market.
The mandatory national standard taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027 sets minimum efficiencies of 23.2%, 23.2% and 23.5% for n-type TOPCon, HJT and BC modules, respectively. On Oct. 16, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) proposed higher thresholds of 23.4%, 23.4% and 23.7% under its draft 2026 Standard Conditions for the PV manufacturing industry.
Separately, China has proposed export controls on 12 photovoltaic technologies including polysilicon, silicon wafer and cell manufacturing technologies as well as the technology management of core equipment.
According to the proposal, certain technologies such as perovskite tandem cells would be categorized as prohibited exports, while TOPCon, back-contact and heterojunction technologies would be subject to export restrictions where specified thresholds are met.
One market analyst expected limited impact on China’s solar product exports, as the new export controls primarily target manufacturing technologies rather than finished products.
The analyst said the measures could reinforce China’s technological leadership by restricting the transfer of proprietary know-how, particularly as overseas markets increasingly push to localize solar manufacturing. This could also benefit Chinese vertically integrated solar manufacturers by preserving their technological advantage, the source said.
However, tighter controls could complicate overseas manufacturing capacity expansions, joint ventures, technology licensing and equipment shipments involving restricted production know-how. Additional registration and licensing requirements could extend project lead times and introduce uncertainty, the analyst added.
OPIS is a specialist business within Dow Jones Energy, a global energy intelligence business that brings together trusted price reporting, research and market intelligence across the energy value chain. OPIS publishes the
OPIS Global Solar Markets Service
, which includes pricing data for solar panels and components across Asia, Europe and the U.S., manufacturing capacity data, module forward curves, and a global solar policy tracker.

title: Bangladesh issues special ordinance to accelerate distributed solar deployment - pv magazine Global
content:
Bangladesh has issued a special ordinance to facilitate private-sector investment in rooftop solar installations on government buildings under Opex and Capex models, as the country seeks to accelerate renewable energy deployment.
Under the Capex model, project owners finance and own the solar installations, while under the Opex model, third-party developers finance, install and operate the systems, with consumers typically paying for the electricity generated under long-term agreements.
The Special Solar Power Installation Ordinance, 2026, is intended to support the government’s ambitious target of adding 3 GW to 4 GW of renewable energy capacity before next summer.
The ordinance, published in the official gazette on Monday, aims to address regulatory gaps that have hindered rooftop solar deployment on government-owned buildings across the country.
In a statement following the ordinance’s approval, the Cabinet Division said existing legislation lacked clear provisions governing long-term electricity tariffs, rooftop rental payments and maintenance arrangements under Opex and Capex models. Cabinet Secretary Nasimul Gani said the ordinance addresses these issues.
The new rules cover solar power systems with capacities of up to 5 MW at government, semi-government, autonomous and local government institutions, state-owned companies and residential buildings.
Eligible installations include rooftop solar, solar-powered irrigation pumps, solar cold storage facilities, electric vehicle charging stations, floating solar and agrivoltaic systems. The ordinance also covers installations on tea garden rooftops, adjacent vacant land, courtyards and other suitable sites.
“A tripartite agreement shall be executed among the consumer, the service provider, and the appropriate authority for the purpose of installing and operating a special solar electricity system under this ordinance,” the ordinance states.
To accelerate project implementation, the ordinance also exempts relevant procurement processes from mandatory use of the Electronic Government Procurement (e-GP) system.
Private-sector investors have welcomed the ordinance, saying it could stimulate rooftop solar investment, although they have called for further measures to address remaining barriers.
Mostafa Al Mahmud, president of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association (BSREA), said the ordinance demonstrates the government’s growing commitment to renewable energy, particularly rooftop solar. “The ordinance will definitely bring some success in power generation,” he said. “However, there are some bottlenecks in it. If those could be removed, perhaps a better output could have been achieved.”
Imran Chowdhury, a director of BSREA, described the ordinance as a timely measure to accelerate distributed solar deployment by making rooftops, unused land and other suitable spaces available for private-sector investment. He said the introduction of Capex and Opex models, alongside simplified procurement procedures, could mobilize investment and shorten project development timelines.
The provision allowing limited tendering for Capex projects valued at up to BDT 50 million ($404.8 million) could also speed up procurement, he added.
However, Chowdhury said greater clarity on bidder eligibility, technical qualifications and participation procedures would be essential to ensure transparent and competitive private-sector participation. “While the ordinance creates promising opportunities for local solar developers, EPC contractors and investors, smaller project sizes may offer limited commercial attraction for foreign investors unless projects can be aggregated into larger, bankable portfolios,” he said.
