title: Researchers scale flexible perovskite modules to 750 cm² with certified 20.2% efficiency
content:
Researchers scale flexible perovskite modules to 750 cm² with certified 20.2% efficiency
Researchers at Soochow University, Southeast University, Linköping University, the Institute of Chemistry of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and
SunFlex New Energy
have developed a way to make large flexible perovskite solar modules that keep most of the efficiency of small cells. The modules are built on flexible PET/ITO substrates.
Efficiency and stability have typically dropped sharply as flexible perovskite devices get larger, and the problem lies at the substrate surface. On flexible ITO, the hydroxyl groups that anchor the self-assembled monolayer (SAM) hole-transport molecule, Me-4PACz, are fewer and less uniform, and they are quickly lost in the polar precursor solution. The perovskite colloids also interact with the SAM’s phosphonic acid groups, which slows SAM anchoring until the hydroxyls are gone. The team added a “decoupling agent”, 3,5-bis(methylsulfonyl)phenylammonium iodide (BSAI), to the precursor. It binds to the lead-iodide species, weakens their interaction with the SAM so the SAM anchors quickly and uniformly, and also slows perovskite nucleation to promote oriented crystal growth.
Third-party certified efficiencies were 26.9% for small-area flexible cells (against 26.22% previously reported), 22.3% for a 14.55 cm² device, 20.6% for an 80 cm² device and 20.2% for a 750 cm² module. The certified 750 cm² device used a phenethylammonium iodide passivator. With a different passivator, 1,3-diaminopropane dihydroiodide, a 14.55 cm² device with 22.0% efficiency lost about 8% after 1,044 hours of maximum power point tracking at 85°C and 65% relative humidity. The devices also passed all test sequences of the IEC TS 63163:2021 standard for flexible portable modules, as certified by TÜV SÜD. The approach also works on rigid substrates and with other SAM molecules.
The team worked with SunFlex for about a year to scale production beyond laboratory prototypes. SunFlex was founded by Yongfang Li, one of the paper’s authors, and builds on perovskite research at Soochow University.

title: TNO, Perovion and Toyo Seikan sign Statement of Intent to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells
content:
TNO, Perovion and Toyo Seikan sign Statement of Intent to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells
Perovion Technologies
and Toyo Seikan Group Holdings have signed a Statement of Intent to advance their joint development of lightweight, flexible perovskite solar cells toward industrialization. The signing took place at a ceremony at the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. The three organizations had already been working together on the technology and on opportunities for practical application, and have now agreed on a joint development roadmap.
Under the roadmap, they will collaborate on technology development, materials development, manufacturing processes and module technologies. Perovion contributes the flexible perovskite solar cell technology developed at TNO and its scalable roll-to-roll manufacturing approach. Toyo Seikan will bring its expertise in advanced functional materials, developed under its MiraNeo brand, as well as its know-how in manufacturing and module integration.
Perovion’s CEO Stefan van de Beek pointed in particular to Toyo Seikan’s encapsulation materials. TNO remains involved as technology and R&D partner, supporting further development and scale-up. The release does not give financial terms, a timeline or production targets.
Perovion is a TNO spin-off, launched in March 2026, that aims to industrialize flexible perovskite solar cells printed on thin foils. It plans a roll-to-roll factory in the Netherlands, with construction planned for 2030, and said at launch that it was seeking investors and industrial partners. TNO also recently unveiled a

title: 黑龙江省黑河市开展光伏发电标准化宣传普及活动-索比光伏网
content:
为深入推进清洁能源标准化建设，普及绿色能源标准知识，依托第57个世界标准日宣传契机，近日，黑龙江省黑河市围绕光伏发电、清洁能源利用、绿色低碳发展主题，扎实开展光伏发电标准化宣传普及活动。
活动聚焦光伏发电工程建设、设备质量、安全运维、节能降耗、并网管理等重点标准内容，通过线下宣讲、展板宣传、发放科普资料、企业走访答疑等多种形式，面向新能源企业、在建光伏项目、产业园区及社会群众开展标准化宣传。重点解读光伏发电国家、行业及先进地方标准规范，讲解标准化在提升光伏项目安全性、经济性、稳定性中的重要作用，引导经营主体严格按照标准开展建设、运维和管理。
同时，结合南北标准协同发展工作，积极对标粤港澳大湾区清洁能源先进标准和成熟管理经验，宣传推广光伏产业规范化、节约化、绿色化发展模式，指导企业以标准引领降本增效、防范安全风险、提升项目质量。
通过本次世界标准日宣传活动，进一步提升了光伏行业从业人员标准意识、规范意识和质量安全意识，有效夯实黑河市清洁能源产业标准化发展基础，助力全市绿色低碳产业高质量发展。

title: 天津：“十五五”新增用电全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决-索比光伏网
content:
10月22日上午，天津市政府新闻办举行“开局起步‘十五五’”系列主题新闻发布会，介绍“十五五”时期我市能源发展有关情况。
市发展改革委主任梁军介绍，能源保障和安全事关国计民生。“十四五”以来，天津深入践行“四个革命、一个合作”能源安全新战略，着力强基础、调结构、优布局、育动能，能源高质量发展迈出坚实步伐。“十四五”期间，能源发展成效主要体现在四个方面。一是保障能力更强，渤海油田稳居全国第一大原油生产基地，原油增量占全国总增量的约40%。电力供应水平稳步提高，电力装机较2020年增长73.7%。二是能源结构更绿，新能源超过煤电成为第一大电源，煤炭消费比重由34.6%下降至24.6%，非化石能源消费比重由7.1%提高至17%，绿电交易连续三年倍速增长。三是设施布局更优，天然气主干架构持续巩固，三座LNG接收站投产运行，接收能力领跑全国。特高压输电网络加速构建，500千伏电网建成双环网结构。四是发展动能更新，获批京津冀燃料电池汽车示范城市群，打造天津港保税区氢能示范产业园，依托荣程集团等企业加快交通领域氢能应用场景建设，燃料电池实证试验平台纳入国家首批能源领域氢能试点，“制储运加用”氢能全产业链发展格局加快形成。
“十五五”时期是我国加快构建新型能源体系、建设能源强国的重要时期。我们将认真落实党中央决策部署和国家发展改革委、国家能源局工作要求，以保安全、优结构、强产业、降成本为主线，着力打造区域能源保障枢纽和能源领域新质生产力发展引领区，到2030年，初步建成以非化石能源为增量供应主体、化石能源为兜底保障、新型电力系统为关键支撑、绿色智慧节约为用能导向的清洁低碳安全高效的新型能源体系，更好支撑经济社会高质量发展。为了实现以上目标，我们在任务安排方面突出“四个着力”。
一是着力筑牢能源安全根基，全面提升综合保障能力。加强与煤炭主产区合作，扎实做好煤炭稳供保运。大力推动渤海油田、大港油田稳产增储，打造全国油气资源保障供给中心和重要LNG接收区;建成天津LNG外输管道复线等项目，持续巩固国产气、进口气相结合，陆上气、LNG相补充的多源多向供气保障格局。健全多层次能源储备体系，强化天然气、成品油、煤炭等能源储备，扎实推进大港油田储气库群项目建设，力争储气库工作气量达到50亿立方米。增强供热、燃气综合保障能力，改造供热管网3000公里以上、燃气管网2000公里以上。
二是着力推进绿色低碳发展，强化生产消费协同转型。统筹推进风电、光伏等非化石能源开发，实施蓟州“风光火热储”多能互补一体化等试点，非化石能源发电装机超过2000万千瓦，装机比重超过50%;持续扩大省间绿电交易，谋划新增绿电入津通道，“十五五”时期新增用电需求全部通过本地绿电和外受电解决。全面落实大气污染治理攻坚行动部署，加快化石能源消费绿色转型，高水平高质量做好节能降碳，煤炭消费总量较2025年下降10%、比重降至21%左右，非化石能源消费比重增至22.2%。
三是着力构建新型电力系统，推进供给水平质效双升。发挥好传统火电兜底保障作用，进一步提高外受电规模，有序实施杨柳青电厂、大唐盘山电厂容量替代，电力装机超过4000万千瓦。抢抓“六张网”建设机遇，打造新型电网平台，建成大同—天津南特高压交流输电工程，推进黑龙江—天津特高压直流输电工程实施，构建“三交一直”特高压输电网络;建设500千伏加强型双环网，推进电网数字化智能化转型。加快蓟州龙潭沟、西大峪抽水蓄能电站开工建设，统筹布局200万千瓦新型储能电站，推进长时储能与快速响应协同联动。提升需求侧协同能力，创新发展虚拟电厂、算电协同、车网互动等新业态。
四是着力推进科技产业创新，前瞻布局发展未来能源。发展壮大新一代风电光伏，打造风电高端装备制造产业集群、全国领先的硅片—光伏组件一体化制造业集群。积极提升新型储能产业能级，前瞻布局固态电池、钠离子电池等新型储能产业。加快构建氢能全链条产业生态，抢抓京津冀城市群氢能综合应用试点机遇，加快输氢、加氢基础设施建设，有序拓展交通、石化、建筑、钢铁等领域用氢场景，高标准建设天津港保税区氢能产业园，壮大氢能装备产业集群。培育发展绿氨、绿色甲醇、可持续航空燃料产业，打造北方国际航运绿色液体燃料加注贸易物流中心。
下一步，我们将锚定发展目标，聚焦能源强国战略导向和“双碳”要求，全力加快全市新型能源体系建设，推动区域能源保障枢纽能级持续提升、能源领域新质生产力发展聚势增效，为全面建设社会主义现代化大都市、奋力谱写中国式现代化天津篇章提供坚实能源支撑，为能源强国建设贡献天津力量。

title: 利好！欧盟废止对华这一光伏领域双反关税-索比光伏网
content:
当地时间2026年10月21日，欧盟委员会发布公告，正式废止对原产于中国太阳能玻璃的最终反倾销税、反补贴税，措施于《欧盟官方公报》公布次日，即10月22日起生效。本次取消关税的产品为钢化钠钙平板太阳能玻璃，对应欧盟海关编码ex 7007 19 80 及相关TARIC编码，设置铁含量、透光率、耐热、抗热冲击、机械强度等技术指标。
欧盟表示，取消关税的核心原因是欧盟境内已无活跃的太阳能玻璃生产企业，双反措施失去设立初衷。退税方面，自2025年7月22日复审启动日起缴纳的相关关税，进口商可按欧盟海关规定申请退还，退税不计利息。此前该品类反倾销税区间17.5%–75.4%，普遍税率67.1%；反补贴税区间3.2%–17.1%，普遍税率17.1%。此次关税废止，将降低中国太阳能玻璃进入欧盟市场的门槛，利好光伏玻璃出口。

title: Submarine cable installation begins for Sicily-Calabria power connection
content:
Submarine cable installation has begun on the "Bolano-Annunziata"
power line, a project that will connect Sicily and Calabria through a 380
kV AC electricity connection.
According to Terna the link is expected to increase electricity exchange
capacity between the island and mainland Italy to 2,000 MW, supporting
greater integration of renewable energy into the grid.
The project includes the installation of three submarine cables, each measuring
7.5 km in length and laid at depths of up to 250 metres.
According to the announcement, the project marks the first time 380 kV
alternating current submarine cables with XLPE insulation have been installed
on Italy’s national transmission grid.
Two underground cable links are also being constructed to connect the submarine
cable landings with the Annunziata and Bolano substations. The onshore
routes will extend approximately 3 km in Sicily and 500 metres in Calabria.
Construction is also progressing on the new Annunziata substation and the
expansion of the Bolano substation.
The project represents a key milestone in strengthening electricity transmission
infrastructure between Sicily and mainland Italy while enabling the continued
expansion of renewable energy capacity.

title: Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval
content:
Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval TGS 4C | 4C Offshore News
Bornholm Energy Island link moves closer after government approval
Denmark’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Utilities has approved a project
that will allow Bornholm’s electricity grid to be connected to the planned
Bornholm Energy Island. The decision follows a political agreement reached
in February 2026.
“Our analyses show that the solution is both technically feasible and
can contribute to a robust electricity supply," says Klaus Winther,
Vice President of System Operations at Energinet.
Energinet and TREFOR Elnet Øst are now progressing preparations for the
connection. The project aims to strengthen Bornholm’s long-term electricity
supply as demand is expected to rise through electrification, the green
transition and new business opportunities.
Bornholm is currently supplied mainly through an electricity cable to Sweden,
which is expected to remain in service until 2035. The island’s peak electricity
demand is around 50 MW, while upgrades to the Swedish connection are expected
to increase available capacity to 57 MW.

title: The Argument in Favor of Tranched Rounds
content: Before we get to today’s column, the big day is here: Anthropic dropped its long-awaited public S-1 filing Monday morning . Tune in today for stories from my colleagues and me that will be breaking down the most important takeaways from the filing, such as improvements in the company’s compute efficiency, details on its spending and cash burn, and interesting new disclosures that could point to an eventual end to its unusual Long-Term Benefit Trust, a group of non-shareholders who advise the company on safety and social issues and can appoint a majority of its board. Onto today’s column... It seems like every AI startup financing these days has multiple tranches in which different investors get in at different valuations. At first, it was unusual to see just two tranches. Now we see extra-hot funding rounds with three tranches or more . It’s no secret that investors aren’t thrilled about these multi-tranche rounds (specifically, the investors that can’t get in at the lower valuation). Some of them argue that the practice allows bigger venture capital firms to flex their power and force smaller VC firms into the second, more expensive tranche. They also say it allows the startup to claim a bigger valuation, even though some or most of the new capital came in at a lower price. But founders and many investors tell me that the unique capital needs of AI companies, which are eternally starved of enough servers, is driving these unusual structures. A young startup that wants to rent around 2,500 Nvidia chips to develop new models might need to raise anywhere between $150 million to $200 million in capital just to rent those graphics processing units from a cloud provider for two years, according to an investor who has backed multiple such companies. The startup then faces two unattractive options: raise capital at a lower valuation to attract institutional investors and heavily dilute existing shareholders, or raise at a $1 billion-plus valuation to minimize dilution but turn off investors that presumably want a bigger return on their investment. Tranched rounds give founders the best of both worlds, as large corporate investors like Nvidia tend to pile into the higher-valued tranche, the investor said. In many cases, Nvidia will provide a significant chunk of capital in the higher-valued tranche, often more than 25% of the total tranche, they said. Then the question becomes how the company can get an institutional investor to lead the higher-priced, less attractive round, as Nvidia doesn’t historically lead rounds itself. (That’s for several reasons, including that Nvidia often invests in competitors, doesn’t want to be seen as setting the price for the round and likely doesn’t want to invite regulatory scrutiny for investing in its customers.) In the hottest rounds, some VCs might not have a choice than to invest in or lead the more expensive round. In other cases, more unusual things might happen. One investor told me their firm will sometimes put the vast majority of their investment into the lower-priced tranche, but then will invest a few million into the higher-priced tranche and “lead” it in name only. That way, it gives corporate investors the cover to pour millions of dollars into the more expensive tranche without having to take on the responsibility of “leading” it and facing scrutiny if the startup goes south, the investor said. Here’s what else is going on… Big Number DeepSeek has closed its second funding round, raising 106 billion yuan ($15.9 billion) in one of the biggest-ever fundraising deals in China’s AI sector, The Information reported. OpenAI is aiming to close a $30 billion fundraising round that will value the AI company at up to $1.25 trillion, not including the new investment, before the end of next week. Deals and Debuts See The Information’s Generative AI Database for an exclusive list of private companies and their investors. Huixi Intelligence , a Beijing chipmaker, closed combined Pre-B+ and Series B funding rounds of undisclosed amounts led by the Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund , taking its 2026 equity financing past 2.5 billion yuan (about $375 million). Pathos AI , which uses AI to develop oncology drugs, raised $237 million in a Series E funding round at a $3 billion post-money valuation, led by Bristol Myers Squibb. Warp Sciences , which uses AI and robotics to speed up drug-candidate chemistry, emerged from stealth with $215 million in funding at an $865 million post-money valuation, led by Lightspeed Venture Partners. Tractian , a 7-year-old physical AI startup based in Atlanta, Georgia, has raised $130 million at a valuation of $1.4 billion in a Series D funding round led by Sapphire Ventures . Promaxo , which combines AI and robotics for prostate care technology, closed the initial tranche of a Series C funding round — amount undisclosed — with participation from New Science Ventures and Amara Ventures , alongside a separate $100 million loan arrangement with an undisclosed lender. Formic , a robots-as-a-service platform for manufacturers, raised $50 million in financing, made up of a $40 million Series B led by Mercato Partners. Cognitive Credit , which provides AI-powered credit-market data and analytics, raised $40 million in a strategic growth investment led by Summit Partners. Higgsfield , an AI video and image generation platform, extended its Series B funding round with new investment from TCV and NVIDIA. Enact , a Zurich robotics startup, emerged from stealth with $30 million in pre-seed funding led by Redalpine , Notion Capital and Firstminute Capital. Maxinsights , which creates training data for robots using footage from cameras worn by contractors, raised $30 million in a seed funding round led by Peak XV. Mave , which is developing an AI tool to automate security investigations, raised $28 million in a Series A funding round led by Red Dot Capital Partners. Slingshot Insurance , an AI-native embedded-insurance platform, emerged from stealth with $27 million in seed funding led by Rally Ventures and Skyward Group. FORT Robotics , which helps develop safety software for physical AI, secured approximately $20 million in new commitments from existing investors, led by Tiger Global with participation from Mark Cuban Companies . Cuttable , an AI advertising platform, raised A$20 million (about $13 million) in a Series A funding round led by Airtree Ventures. Modelyo , which lets companies run AI in the cloud without exposing their data, raised approximately $17 million in funding led by OlivTree . Electric vehicles company Rivian acquired Third Dimension AI , a developer of AI-powered 3D spatial generation, to speed up synthetic data generation and full-world simulation for its driver-assistance and self-driving systems. Albert Invent , an AI platform for materials R&D, secured a growth equity investment from Applied Ventures , the venture arm of Applied Materials , in an amount the company didn't disclose. Hugging Face releases Carbon-X , an AI model that lets users ask questions about DNA sequences and their health and get a natural language response. Moonshot AI on Friday announced its new model, Kimi K3.1 Pro , demonstrating performance that rivals that of top-tier U.S. frontier models on some benchmarks. Walmart launched Agent Gateway, a connector that allows AI agents to browse Walmart’s website and make purchases. The launch comes as Walmart’s competitor, Amazon , has blocked AI agents. Canva , a graphic design platform, launched Craft , its first AI model for generating images trained on human-designed templates within Canva. OpenAI ’s systems had multiple vulnerabilities that would allow AI agents to circumvent monitoring and take arbitrary unauthorized actions, evaluators from AI safety nonprofits METR and Redwood Research found during a three-week pilot with OpenAI, according to a report released Wednesday. OpenAI also made its Decisions API model, a classifier model meant to Jev , widely available. title: Stripe’s AI Shopping Lead Puts Card Giants on Edge
content: As AI assistants like Instinct and Meta Platforms’ Muse start to gain traction in shopping, Stripe has taken a leading position in how the agents pay. That’s putting the credit card giants on edge. The reason for their apprehension: Stripe in many cases is enabling AI agent purchases through virtual cards for one-time use, which can leave card networks with less control over the shopping and payment process, people who work closely with the card firms say. Mastercard and Visa have developed their own payment technology for agent shopping that would use customers’ existing cards, giving the card companies more visibility into who’s making what purchases. That method is still at an early stage, though. When people shop online themselves, they typically enter their card details or choose a saved payment method at checkout. But when an agent makes a purchase, it needs a way to handle shoppers’ payment information securely and use it across different retailers. Agents also need guardrails to ensure they don’t make accidental splurges. Meta and Instinct both have found a solution to those needs in Stripe’s Link digital wallet, which securely stores the users’ own card or bank account details. To enable the agent making a payment, Stripe issues a single-use virtual card that has a spending limit tied to a purchase the user has approved. The agent never sees the users’ actual card number, and the card’s limit keeps the agent from overspending. The merchant accepts the virtual card as it would any other card payment, while Stripe separately charges the user’s credit card to cover the cost of the purchase. That process creates two card transactions for a given purchase and can make it harder to connect the user with the actual purchase the agent makes. One person familiar with Mastercard’s thinking said agents’ use of virtual cards has created concerns in part because it can make it harder for card networks, banks and merchants to track transactions from start to finish and resolve disputed charges. Card networks and banks rely on users’ transaction histories to spot risky or fraudulent transactions. The use of virtual cards also puts Stripe in an advantageous position in AI shopping. It could gain more insight into people’s agentic shopping habits than the card networks currently can, since Stripe can see what people are buying through the AI agents it supports. And its early foothold could give it more sway than the card networks over how the technology evolves. “For Visa and Mastercard, the biggest risk to their business is Stripe infrastructure becoming the default solution,” said Rene Reinsberg, CEO and co-founder of Self, a startup that builds identity and payments tools for AI agents. “I think that’s even more pronounced with agentic commerce than the traditional commerce checkout flows.” Shopping with agents is still in its infancy, but it has begun to take off with early AI adopters. Last week, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, for instance, told investors that more than a quarter of the 10 million users of Muse are shopping with the app, making commerce its most popular use. The average size of Muse transactions is over $200, he said. The demand for shopping with the app has so exceeded Meta’s expectations that it had to work with Stripe in the week after Muse launched to raise credit limits due to high shopping volumes, Zuckerberg said. In another wrinkle, Stripe could switch an agent’s card to a different card network from the shopper’s original card—for instance, the agent might pay with a Visa virtual card that’s funded by the user’s Mastercard card. That could divert transactions and fees away from the card network for the shopper’s original card. Stripe works with both Visa and Mastercard in its broader card issuing business, though it isn’t clear how transaction volume is divided between the card giants for virtual card agentic payments. Visa and Mastercard, for their part, are promoting their own alternative to virtual cards by creating digital tokens tied to shoppers’ existing cards that authorized agents can use to make purchases. The tokens identify the end user without the agent handling sensitive card information directly. Both card giants are courting AI companies and merchants to use their respective payment systems, Visa Intelligent Commerce and Mastercard Agent Pay. Visa, for example, launched a pilot with Bill and Billtrust, companies that help businesses manage or collect payments, that allows authorized agents to pay invoices approved by buyers. Visa and Mastercard also partnered with Anthropic to help merchants build their own AI shopping assistants using Claude technology. While the technology is already in use in some transactions and pilot launches—and Stripe has added support for Visa and Mastercard tokens—adoption remains limited overall. But the card networks may have an edge in winning over card-issuing banks to the token system. The banks are another crucial part of card payments and would be key allies because they control the approval that determines whether card transactions happen at all. Last month, Bank of America and five other banks published proposed industry guidelines that appeared to favor the card networks’ preferred approach over Stripe’s use of virtual cards. The banks called for “auditable methods to enter payment credentials.” The banks didn’t call out virtual cards specifically as a risk, but they did warn about agentic payment methods that make it harder to connect a purchase to an actual shopper or merchant. Stripe, for its part, says it has worked closely with its card network partners on its current technology. “Stripe built this [virtual card] capability in consultation with our network partners and will continue to work closely with them as standards for agentic commerce evolve,” a Stripe spokesperson said. A Mastercard spokesperson said different payment methods could “coexist” as agentic commerce matures, but Mastercard believes over the long term that “the model will increasingly be tokenized transactions routed directly with the merchant.” That approach “preserves the right information flow between the consumer, merchant and issuer, supports clearer dispute resolution, and allows the merchant of record to manage the relationship with the cardholder,” the Mastercard spokesperson said. Visa didn’t have a comment.

title: Anthropic’s Big Reveal
content: The tech industry equivalent of the Super Bowl may finally be upon us. Anthropic could make public the paperwork for its initial public offering as early as Monday. Details about Anthropic’s finances from either drafts of the IPO filing or recent investor meetings have been dribbling out for weeks. As a result, some of the S-1’s revelations will not be, well, all that revelatory. But there are still many, many mysteries about Anthropic the filing could clear up, or at least make a little less fuzzy. I asked my colleagues Jason Dean and Laura Mandaro for their shortlist of items they hope the S-1 will illuminate: • More financial details. More clarity on Anthropic’s trajectory toward profitability, along with cash flow numbers and other operational financial metrics that haven’t yet leaked out. • Ownership, investment and revenue details from big partners. Hopefully, the filing will confirm just how much money Anthropic is paying Google and Amazon to run its AI on their servers, along with details about how much those companies invested in Anthropic and how much those stakes have appreciated. • Who pays Anthropic’s bills. Anthropic has said around a fifth of its revenue this quarter of its revenue in the first half of this year came from just two customers, compared to a quarter for all of 2025, according to published reports. Investors will look for more recent concentration data and additional details on the sources of its revenue. Historically, most of its revenue has come from sales of its AI via an application programming interface, but these can rise and fall depending on what model is hot among developers. We’re looking for details on revenue from its Claude subscriptions as well as through other companies like Amazon that resell Anthropic AI in exchange for a cut of those sales . • More on governance. Many idiosyncrasies of Anthropic’s mission-minded corporate structure are public. For instance, a group of non-shareholders called the Long-Term Benefit Trust appoints the majority of its board. As we’ve reported , in the run-up to the IPO, Anthropic developed a plan to grant its seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, a combined 50.1% of voting power even if they reduce some of their stakes. What we don’t know is whether Amodei has any particular power over the six other founders and how exactly Anthropic will resolve conflicts between the trust and board members appointed by the founders. (Anthropic has planned to give employees a special class of stock for tiebreaker votes—complicated!) • Lockups and secondary sales. We’ve written that Anthropic has mulled extending the lockups —the period when most shareholders are barred from selling their stock—beyond the typical 180-day period. But the company has considered making an exception for some shareholders at the time of the IPO, allowing what’s known as a secondary sale at the listing. Such sales would contrast with other tech IPOs this year that didn’t allow secondary sales during their listings, such as SpaceX and Cerebras. We’re looking for how long most investors have to sit on their shares and which groups of investors—or employees—can bail more quickly. More Ahead The Anthropic filing fireworks aren’t the only big events in tech we’ll be watching next week. There’s also: • Earnings reports from the three major hyperscalers. Google and Microsoft are scheduled to report on Wednesday, while Amazon will report on Thursday. Any changes the companies announce to their data center spending plans or forecasts about AI demand are likely to move the already jittery markets. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy isn’t waiting until earnings to strike a bullish note on the performance of AWS, his cloud unit. In an Andreessen Horowitz podcast published Friday, Jassy said AWS is “largely sold out” of computing capacity through the end of next year. He also said the company’s decade-old acquisition of Annapurna Labs, a semiconductor startup behind AWS’ custom AI chip and other processors, may end up being Amazon’s best deal ever. • Instacart’s next move. On Friday, we broke the news that Instacart is exploring a possible sale of the company and has held preliminary conversations with DoorDash and Uber. Our story said that talks with Uber appear to have fizzled. But it will be interesting to see if a deal with someone else comes together. Instacart and DoorDash are due to report earnings on Nov. 5 and 4, respectively. Expect analysts to grill the companies about the prospects for a deal, if one isn’t announced by then. • New Apple devices. Apple is having an event on Wednesday where it’s expected to announce its first touchscreen MacBook, as we mentioned earlier in the week . Get ready for some greasy MacBook screens. In Other News AI has delivered no financial payoff to U.S. companies other than tech companies, Torsten Slock, chief economist at private equity firm Apollo Global Management argued in an essay . China’s Moonshot AI on Friday announced a new model , Kimi K3.1 Pro, that rivals the performance of leading U.S. frontier models on some benchmarks. title: Exclusive: Inside Unusual Machines' $52 Million Drone Battery Acquisition
content: In 2020, Matt Barnard built a drone by hand at his home in Missouri and thought he had the perfect buyers for it: cattle ranchers in neighboring Oklahoma, who he knew had a heck of a time keeping track of their grazing herds. Using drones equipped with cameras, ranchers could follow their cattle on their laptops. But then the ranchers came up with a competing way to locate the cattle—GPS devices clipped to the animals’ ears—and lost any interest in Barnard’s drones. If he couldn’t sell drones, Barnard thought he might be able to produce and sell the primary component that makes them go—batteries. He launched a startup designing battery packs specifically for drones. The bet paid off last week, when Barnard closed the sale of that startup, Upgrade Energy, to Florida drone component supplier Unusual Machines for $52 million in cash and stock. It was a coup for Barnard, who told me he had entirely bootstrapped the business and raised no venture capital or debt. The deal was also a big get for Unusual Machines, which added to its muscle as the leading supplier of U.S.-made drone components to companies competing in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program for $1.1 billion in contracts. Chinese manufacturers such as DJI make most of the world’s drones, along with the components that go into them. But the Pentagon, seeking to build up a U.S. drone industry and wean the country off Chinese suppliers, has sharply restricted the use of Chinese-made components by Drone Dominance participants. In the latest stage of the Drone Dominance competition last month, Unusual Machines supplied components to four of the nine companies that placed, including top winners Perennial Autonomy, founded by former Google Chair Eric Schmidt, and Neros Technologies. The acquisition of Upgrade Energy, which is also a supplier to Perennial and Neros, bulks up Unusual Machines’ manufacturing capacity with the most expensive single component in a drone—the battery. Unusual Machines’ shares are up 21% since it announced the deal in May, and they’ve risen 32% over the last year. “We exist because we took this gamble and people invested in this gamble,” Allan Evans, CEO of Unusual Machines, told me. “We’re a little past it being a gamble—it’s worked out and now we’re scaling.” I visited Upward’s factory in Torrance, Calif., earlier this month. It’s a large, white-painted space in an industrial park where after work a group of young men sitting on a couch huddled together over a videogame and otherwise hung out. The factory itself was through a door in the back. There, in rows of desks packed with electronics, some 50 workers package next-generation cylindrical cells from Taiwan’s Molicel, Calif.–based Amprius Technologies and others in black, rectangular packs small enough to hold in one hand. They then box them up and move them on pallets to a loading dock. Barnard said they are pumping out 400 packs a day. Next-generation battery startups began to pop up in the late 2000s and the early 2010s, triggered by improvements in lithium-ion batteries and especially the rise of Tesla. In 2020 and 2021, a slew of them went public on the general expectation of an electric vehicle boom. But EV sales beyond Tesla remained sluggish. The industry is only now coming out of that malaise. The drone boom, along with the mania over AI data centers, have been the main life preservers for these startups, as we have reported . But Barnard has been in the business longer than most, pumping out drone packs. His big insight was to avoid the risks most of the other battery startups took in attempting to invent and scale up a new battery chemistry or component. He decided to take some of the best of what was already out there—like the batteries made by Molicel and Amprius, with their next-generation silicon anodes—and figure out how to package them optimally for drones. He then got those packs in front of drone makers. In 2023, Barnard said, he got a deal to power drones that delivered food in Georgia for Papa Johns Pizza. The same year, he landed his first significant deal—a contract to supply Neros, at the time a small drone maker based in El Segundo, Calif. Based on that contract, Barnard decided to move Upgrade from Missouri to Southern California. He and his father packed up his things, stuffed them into a big truck, and drove to the state. With three employees, they moved into a space in Compton, Calif. Upgrade got some press when it powered a solar aircraft making a round-the-world flight. Last year, orders for batteries to power combat drones started rolling in. Barnard continued to get business from Neros, which had become one of the country’s main drone manufacturers, and now also had business with Anduril and AeroVironment, he said. Near the end of last year, Evans came around. Barnard recalls Evans saying that Unusual Machines wanted to begin building batteries. “I said, ‘OK, cool. What do you want to do?’ And they’re like, ‘Acquire you.’” “‘Ah, OK, great,’” Barnard recalls responding. Evans said he had to take Barnard out for meals before he could close the deal. “Initially he was like, ‘Nah.’ And so we had dinner a couple of nights,” he said. Evans stressed that he could promise Barnard a ton of business and expansion. “We have the buying volume to be an anchor customer for somebody to move cell production to the U.S.,” he recalled telling Barnard. “We have the ability to automate and scale. We have the ability to put batteries into thousands of drones.” That turned Barnard around. “Now I’m not competing against some other company that just raised $10 million, $20 million, when I did not have $10 million or $20 million sitting around,” Barnard said. “I recognized that to stay competitive, I needed to attach myself to some of that funding. I’m glad I did.” ----- Noteworthy General Motors led a $108 million Series B round in sodium-ion battery systems provider Peak Energy. GM and Peak are developing sodium-ion batteries for deployment on the grid. In total, Peak has raised $173 million in equity funding. High-nickel battery maker Forge Nano went public in a merger with a special purpose acquisition corporation, highlighting the revival of new stock listings in the battery industry after a four-year downturn. The company is building a plant in Morrisville, N.C., to manufacture high-nickel batteries with either silicon or graphite anodes, and it plans to begin production in 2028. title: The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
content:
The Download: everyday AI harms and the race to nuclear spaceflight
Plus: Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivity.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab
We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.
A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.
As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.
Here’s why AI safety needs to go further.
Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships
Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.
A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.
The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off?
Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality.
—Robin George Andrews
This story is part of “Are we there yet?” from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivity
The restrictions disrupted air defences and drone operations. (Politico)
+ Elon Musk says Ukraine violated the terms with offensive drone use. (BBC)
+ Ukraine is now partnering with Nokia on a Starlink alternative. (CNBC)
+ Ukrainian drones hit a Russian government data center. (Tom’s Hardware)
+ A Russian ministry wants to move them underground. (Kyiv Independent)
+ Ukraine’s drones are fueling a wild data market. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Anthropic’s Claude accessed Georgia voter data without approval
Anthropic says the AI bypassed a paywall. (Axios)
+ Mythos 5 recently kept hacking despite warnings of real-world harm. (BI)
+ Chatbots can sway voters better than political ads. (MIT Technology Review)
3 A personalised skin cancer vaccine is set to be approved next year
The mRNA vaccine showed great promise in trials. (New Scientist $)
+ Companies are playing word games with vaccines. (MIT Technology Review)
4 OpenAI is now training frontier models without internet access
It paused training after models breached external systems. (Bloomberg $)
+ Training will now take place offline to reduce security risks. (TechCrunch)
+ Its agents can still communicate without a network connection. (Verge)
5 US lawmakers are preparing for possible AI-driven mass layoffs
A new bill would extend jobless aid and retraining support. (NYT $)
+ But what do the numbers actually say about AI’s impact on jobs? (MIT Technology Review)
6 The first foldable iPhone is drawing buyers…and criticism
Reviewers praised its inner screen but criticised its outer one. (WSJ $)
+ Peter Thiel says Apple has done 'nothing new' after Steve Jobs. (BI)
7 Iran has threatened to target Gulf undersea cables if war resumes
Officials said Tehran would disrupt internet connections. (Reuters $)
8 New UFO files detail a strange, flying "black triangle”
FBI documents describe a 15-foot object moving at fighter-jet speed. (Axios)
+ It’s never been easier to be a conspiracy theorist. (MIT Technology Review)
9 The BBC’s Blue Planet III left flaws in its footage to prove it’s not AI
Producers used murkier shots to reinforce the series’ authenticity. (Guardian)
10 Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey has arrived—to scorn and ridicule
Viewers derided Grok’s first AI-generated episode. (TechCrunch)
Quote of the day
“It's very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry.”
—Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) tells Axios that bombastic claims from AI leaders are failing to win over the public.
One more thing
A woman’s uterus has been kept alive outside the body for the first time
Ten months ago, reproductive health researchers placed a freshly donated human uterus inside a new device they call “Mother.” They connected the organ to the machine’s plastic veins and arteries and pumped in modified human blood.
The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story.
—Jessica Hamzelou
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)
+ In good news for coral reefs, scientists have found some are surprisingly climate-resilient.
+ Decades of joy and movement come alive through these stunning archival photos of American dance floors.
+ Astronaut Jessia Meir has shared a stunning time-lapse view of the southern aurora dancing across the Earth.
+ A college student has turned the Met’s open-access data into a daily game that showcases underrepresented art and artifacts.

title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
content:
The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
Lawmakers are passing industry-backed bills to guard against the worst outcomes, rather than addressing more common problems.
Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.
We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.
A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.
A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.
Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.
We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.
AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.
Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own.
We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.
Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.
Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

title: Rennen mit der Roten Königin: Mit Spieltheorie zu mehr Softwaresicherheit im KI-Zeitalter
content:
Rennen mit der Roten Königin: Mit Spieltheorie zu mehr Softwaresicherheit im KI-Zeitalter

Rennen mit der Roten Königin: Mit Spieltheorie zu mehr Softwaresicherheit im KI-Zeitalter
| Copyright:
CISPA/Chiara Schwarz
Download
In Lewis Carrolls Alice hinter den Spiegeln (1871), trifft Alice auf die Rote Königin und wird von ihr in ein hastiges Rennen verwickelt. In diesem wundersamen Land, erfährt Alice, muss man so schnell wie möglich laufen, nur, um auf der Stelle zu bleiben. Mit diesem „Red Queens Race“ vergleicht Christoph Landolt die Situation von Software-Herstellern im KI-Zeitalter. Denn mit den sprunghaft wachsenden Cyber-Fähigkeiten der Frontier-Modelle multiplizieren sich auch die Angriffsmöglichkeiten. Mit einem Ansatz aus der Spieltheorie hat Landolt berechnet, wie die Veröffentlichung neuer KI-Modelle sequenziert werden kann, um Software-Herstellern einen Vorsprung vor Cyberkriminellen einzuräumen.
Dass sich mit jedem neuen Release die Fähigkeiten der KI-Modelle multiplizieren, ist ein Phänomen, das Christoph Landolt beschäftigt. Er ist Doktorand in der Forschungsgruppe von CISPA-Faculty Prof. Dr. Mario Fritz und beobachtet die Veröffentlichung sogenannter Frontier-Modelle vor allem in Hinblick auf ihre Schadenspotenziale für die Cybersicherheit. „Als Claude Opus 4.6 im Februar 2026 veröffentlicht wurde, hat das Modell allein in den ersten beiden Tagen über 500 schwerwiegende Schwachstellen in Open-Source-Software gefunden. Das zeigt, wie das ganze Feld plötzlich geflutet wird mit neuen Schwachstellen“, sagt er. Kurz darauf, im April 2026, entschied sich Anthropic gegen eine allgemeine Veröffentlichung von Claude Mythos Preview, weil das Modell sich gefährlich effizient darin erwies, bislang unbekannte Sicherheitslücken zu entdecken. „Die Frage, die wir uns in unserer Forschung stellen“, sagt Landolt, „ist, wie verändert diese Dynamik die Art und Weise auf die wir Cybersicherheit im KI-Zeitalter denken müssen?“
Wie gelingt verantwortungsvolle Offenlegung im KI-Zeitalter?
Üblicherweise sorgt die sogenannte verantwortungsvolle Offenlegung für einen Vorsprung der Cybersicherheit gegenüber den Cyberkriminellen. Wenn etwa Forschende eine Schwachstelle entdecken, melden sie diese dem Software-Hersteller, der einen Patch entwickelt und veröffentlicht. Das Wissen über die Schwachstelle dringt also erst zusammen mit dem Update nach außen und die User:innen haben eine faire Chance, sich rechtzeitig zu schützen. Öffentlich verfügbare Frontier-Modelle stellen ihre offensiven und defensiven Fähigkeiten jedoch beiden Seiten gleichzeitig zur Verfügung. „Es ist schwierig zu sagen, ob die klassische Responsible Disclosure im AI-Zeitalter obsolet geworden ist“, sagt Landolt. „Aber wir wissen, dass sich die Zeit, die es braucht, um von einer offengelegten Schwachstelle zu einem Angriff zu kommen, stark reduziert hat. Die Webseite zerodayclock.com zeigte zeitweise, dass es 2018 noch rund 2,3 Jahre waren, 2026 dagegen nur noch rund 10 Stunden.“
Mit der Sequenzierung von KI-Modellen zu mehr Cybersicherheit
Diese Dynamik wirkt sich darauf aus, ob Hersteller das Schließen von Sicherheitslücken – und User:innen das Installieren von Patches – überhaupt noch als sinnhaft erachten. „Wenn die Angreifer schneller neue Schwachstellen entdecken, als die User ihre Software updaten können, beginnt das System zu oszillieren“, erklärt Landolt. Im sprichwörtlichen Red Queen’s Race fallen Software-Hersteller und -User:innen dann zurück, ganz egal, wie schnell sie laufen: „Der Nutzen, einen Patch online zu stellen wird negativ, und der Nutzen, einen Patch nicht online zu stellen, wird ebenfalls negativ. Wenn wir in diesem Bereich operieren, ist es schlecht, egal was wir tun.“ Vor diesem Hintergrund plädiert Landolt dafür, neue Frontier-Modelle schrittweise zu veröffentlichen und Software-Herstellern als Erstes Zugang zu ihnen zu gewähren: „Durch diesen Vorsprung können wir ein Incentive dafür setzen, dass alle Patches schon bereitstehen, wenn ein neues KI-Modell öffentlich zugänglich wird. So könnte ich meine Software wieder sinnvoll schützen.“
Im oben genannten Fall von Claude Mythos Preview entschied sich Anthropic zu einem ähnlichen Vorgehen: Im Rahmen von „Project Glasswing“ wurde das Modell nur ausgewählten US-Techkonzernen zugänglich gemacht. Was Landolt und seine Co-Autor:innen Tobias Lorenz, Marta Kwiatkowska und Mario Fritz in „The Oracle’s Gambit“ vorschlagen, betrifft potenziell die gesamte KI-Industrie: Mit einem Ansatz aus der Spieltheorie, dem Stackelberg-Modell, haben sie berechnet, wie man den Zugang zu neuen Frontier-Modellen optimal im Sinne der Cybersicherheit sequenzieren könnte. „Wir haben keine wissenschaftliche Literatur gefunden, die den Einfluss von neuveröffentlichten KI-Modellen auf die Cybersicherheit analysiert“, erläutert Landolt. „Deswegen haben wir ein Modell aufgestellt, das wir mit einem exakten Wert lösen können, damit wir die Validierung der Community bekommen und Rückmeldung erhalten können, ob es Dynamiken in der Praxis gibt, die wir nicht berücksichtigt haben.“
„The Oracle’s Gambit“: Ein Stackelberg-Spiel auf zwei Ebenen
Mit ihrer Umsetzung des Stackelberg-Modells präsentieren die Forschenden ein strategisches Spiel auf zwei Ebenen. Auf der ersten Ebene tritt das Frontier Lab selbst als Spieler auf. Es schlägt eine Release Policy für ein neues Frontier-Modell vor und bestimmt damit, auf welche Art und Weise die KI veröffentlicht wird. Damit legt es zugleich die Spielregeln fest, nach denen Cyberkriminelle und Software-Hersteller auf der zweiten Ebene gegeneinander antreten. In diesem zweiten Spiel entwickeln die Hersteller mithilfe der KI Patches für eine bestimmte Anzahl von Schwachstellen, während die Cyberkriminellen das Modell dazu verwenden, diese Schwachstellen auszubeuten. Dabei befinden sich die Hersteller in einem strukturellen Nachteil. „Der Verteidiger muss nicht nur Sicherheit gewährleisten, sondern auch Verfügbarkeit: Eine Schwachstelle muss erkannt, ein Patch gebaut und getestet und veröffentlicht werden“, erklärt Landolt. „Der Angreifer hat es leichter, denn ihm ist es egal, ob er einen Absturz herbeiführt.“ Zudem müssen die Hersteller entscheiden, ob sie den Patch veröffentlichen oder zurückhalten. Dies ist eine strategische Abwägung, denn ist der Patch erst einmal bekannt, kann er von der gegnerischen Seite rückentwickelt und für Exploits genutzt werden.
Sobald dieses Spiel zu einem abschließenden Wert kommt, fällt der nächste Spielzug zurück an das Frontier Lab. Es muss nun eine Veröffentlichungsstrategie finden, die das größtmögliche gesellschaftliche Wohlergehen verspricht. Im Modell von Landolt und seinen Kolleg:innen ist das Frontier Lab dabei nicht allein von Altruismus, sondern auch von wirtschaftlichen Anreizen motiviert. „Disclosure Policies bei Software-Herstellern gehen in der Regel davon aus, dass die Entwickler selbst ein maximales Interesse daran haben, ihre User zu schützen. Bei einem Frontier Lab ist die Kundenbindung aber eine andere, denn die User einer Software sind ja nicht unbedingt Kunden des Frontier Labs“, erläutert Landolt. „Unser Spiel sieht vor, dass das Frontier Lab die Opportunity Costs seines verpassten Marktanteils balanciert mit dem Welfare des ganzen Systems. Die Idee dahinter ist, dass der Reputationsverlust des Frontier Labs sehr hoch sein könnte, wenn seine Modelle für bösartige Zwecke verwendet würden.“ In „The Oracle’s Gambit“ wirken am Gemeinwohl orientierte Veröffentlichungsstrategien also zugleich wirtschaftlichen Einbußen entgegen.
Spieltheorie und Cybersicherheit: Einbezug des Gegenübers
Es ist kein Zufall, dass die Forschenden einen spieltheoretischen Ansatz gewählt haben, um eine sinnvoll sequenzierte Veröffentlichung von Frontier-Modellen zu berechnen. „Cybersecurity und Spieltheorie ist eine gängige Kombination, aus theoretischen Überlegungen heraus. Viele Optimierungsprobleme in der Mathematik gehen von einer starren Umgebung aus. Aber in der Spieltheorie versuchen wir, optimale Lösungen zu finden unter Einbezug des Gegenübers“, sagt Landolt. Dieser Einbezug eines Dritten und der Dynamik, die er in die Interaktion einbringt, hat die Forschenden bei der Modellierung des Spielablaufs jedoch vor logistische Herausforderungen gestellt. „Wenn wir alle möglichen Interaktionen zwischen Angreifer und Verteidiger berücksichtigen, wird unser Spiel zu komplex. Wir mussten also auf vereinfachte Lösungsalgorithmen oder Annahmen zurückgreifen. Und selbst für das vereinfachte Modell haben wir zwei Terrabyte Arbeitsspeicher benötigt, nur um das Spiel einmal lösen zu können.“ Das Ergebnis ihrer Berchnungen präsentieren die Forschenden heute auf der GameSec in Michigan, der weltweit einzigen Konferenz, die Themen und Expert:innen aus Spieltheorie und KI für Sicherheit vereint.

title: Sicherheits-Check: Forschungsteam untersucht kommunale E-Mail-Server im DACH-Raum
content:
Sicherheits-Check: Forschungsteam untersucht kommunale E-Mail-Server im DACH-Raum
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Prof. Dr. Ronald Petrlic bei einem Vortrag auf dem IEEE Symposium on Privacy Expectations in New York Anfang Oktober 2026.
| Quelle:
Lydia Lee
Download
Nutzen Kommunen europäische E-Mail-Provider? Und wie schützen sie sich vor Angreifern im Netz? Um das herauszufinden, analysierte die Technische Hochschule Nürnberg Georg Simon Ohm (Ohm) gemeinsam mit Forschenden der Universität Fribourg und der Hochschule Luzern aus der Schweiz sowie der Technischen Hochschule Ingolstadt über 15.000 E-Mail-Server von Kommunen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz.
Für ihre Analyse verwendeten die Forschenden ausschließlich öffentlich zugängliche Daten aus dem Domain Name System (DNS). Dadurch konnten sie die Tests durchführen, ohne in die untersuchten Systeme einzugreifen.
Ihrer Studie zufolge nutzen lediglich 7,2 Prozent der Kommunen in Deutschland für ihre E-Mail-Kommunikation US-Provider. Damit sind deutsche Kommunen beim Thema digitale Souveränität bereits gut aufgestellt. Auch die Stadt Nürnberg setzt auf einen europäischen E-Mail-Dienst. Anders sieht es in Österreich und der Schweiz aus. Hier liegt der Anteil bei 67 Prozent und 53,3 Prozent.
Die Wahl des Anbieters spiele vor allem mit Blick auf den Schutz sensibler Daten eine wichtige Rolle, erklärt Prof. Dr. Ronald Petrlic von der Fakultät Informatik der Ohm. Kommunale E-Mails enthalten häufig personenbezogene Informationen und weitere schützenswerte Inhalte. Werden diese über US-Anbieter verarbeitet, können sie unter bestimmten rechtlichen Voraussetzungen in den Zugriffsbereich US-amerikanischer Behörden fallen. Der CLOUD Act ermögliche es US-Strafverfolgungsbehörden, elektronische Daten von US-Unternehmen anzufordern – auch wenn diese auf Servern außerhalb der USA gespeichert sind. „Digitale Souveränität bedeutet deshalb, sich damit auseinanderzusetzen, bei welchen Anbietern kommunale Daten verarbeitet werden“, betont Petrlic.
Auch innerhalb Deutschlands gibt es hinsichtlich der digitalen Souveränität regionale Unterschiede. In Bayern liegt der Anteil an Kommunen, die ihre E-Mails über US-Provider versenden, mit 18,7 Prozent über dem bundesweiten Durchschnitt. Petrlic führt das vor allem auf die Nähe zum Microsoft-Sitz in München zurück. Das habe auch Vorteile: „In der Studie haben wir herausgefunden, dass die Kommunen, die Microsoft nutzen, eher etablierte Sicherheitslösungen, beispielsweise gegen ‚Spoofing‘, umgesetzt haben.“ Spoofing bezeichnet eine Betrugsmasche, bei der Angreifer E-Mails versenden, die scheinbar von einer offiziellen kommunalen E-Mail-Adresse stammen.
Denn neben der digitalen Souveränität legte das Forschungsteam sein Augenmerk bei der Studie auf einen weiteren Aspekt: die Cybersicherheit in Kommunen. Sie versuchten herauszufinden, wie einfach es ist, E-Mails zu verfälschen und im Namen der Kommunen zu versenden. Die Ergebnisse zeigen, dass dies bei vielen Verwaltungen möglich ist. Eine wesentliche Ursache hierfür ist, dass etablierte Sicherheitsstandards wie SPF, DKIM und DMARC nicht oder nicht korrekt eingesetzt werden.
„Für Kommunen ist es wichtig, sich einen Überblick zu verschaffen, welche Dienste E-Mails im Namen der Kommunen versenden“, rät Petrlic. Dafür gäbe es Monitoring-Tools, die regelmäßig über die jeweiligen Dienste und IP-Adressen informieren. So lassen sich Angreifer und Missbrauchsquellen frühzeitig erkennen. Unterstützung erhalten die Kommunen auch beim Landesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (LSI) Bayern, das bayerische Kommunen zum Thema Cybersicherheit berät. Auch das Forschungsteam der Ohm steht in regelmäßigem Austausch mit dem LSI Bayern und dem Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI).
Als Ergebnis der Studie sind zwei interaktive Karten entstanden. Interessierte können darauf einsehen, wie die einzelnen Kommunen im DACH-Raum zum Thema Digitale Souveränität und Cybersicherheit aufgestellt sind:

title: Neues HPC-System für Klimaforschung am DKRZ wird von BULL geliefert
content:
Neues HPC-System für Klimaforschung am DKRZ wird von BULL geliefert
Hinweis zur Verwendung von Bildmaterial: Die Verwendung des Bildmaterials zur Pressemitteilung ist bei Nennung der Quelle vergütungsfrei gestattet. Das Bildmaterial darf nur in Zusammenhang mit dem Inhalt dieser Pressemitteilung verwendet werden. Falls Sie das Bild in höherer Auflösung benötigen oder Rückfragen zur Weiterverwendung haben, wenden Sie sich bitte direkt an die Pressestelle, die es veröffentlicht hat.
ICON-Simulation in 5 km Auflösung vom EU-Projekt EERIE. Die Farben zeigen die Meeresoberflächentemperatur, die Schattierung die Strömungsgeschwindigkeit. Der HLRE-5 wird solche Simulationen im Kilometer-Maßstab mit höherer Energieeffizienz ermöglichen.
| Quelle:
Visualisierung: M. Böttinger
| Copyright:
Michael Böttinger, DKRZ
Download
Das Deutsche Klimarechenzentrum (DKRZ) hat Bull, einem führenden Anbieter für Advanced Computing und KI, einen Auftrag im Wert von 40 Millionen Euro für seinen nächsten Supercomputer erteilt. Der Auftrag umfasst neben dem HPC- und Speichersystem auch Supportleistungen über fünf Jahre. Das auf der BullSequana XH3500-Plattform basierende System ist darauf ausgelegt, sowohl physikalische Simulationen als auch KI-gestützte Klimaforschung zu ermöglichen und dabei die Energieeffizienz gegenüber dem Vorgängersystem deutlich zu verbessern.
Das Hochleistungsrechnersystem für Erdsystemforschung (HLRE-5) soll voraussichtlich Anfang 2028 für die Nutzerinnen und Nutzer zur Verfügung stehen und wird in der Lage sein, zwei globale Klimasimulationen mit einer Auflösung von 5 km gleichzeitig auszuführen. Dabei soll der Energiebedarf pro simuliertem Jahr gegenüber dem derzeitigen System Levante um rund 75 Prozent sinken.
Dieses Engagement für Energieeffizienz ist nicht neu, sondern baut auf jahrelangen kontinuierlichen gemeinsamen Anstrengungen von DKRZ und Bull auf. Die aktuelle GPU-Erweiterung des Levante-Systems erreichte in den Ausgaben der Green500-Liste vom November 2025 und Juni 2026 den dritten Platz unter den energieeffizientesten Supercomputern der Welt. Die ersten beiden Plätze gingen ebenfalls an Systeme von Bull.
„Mit dem neuen System können wir den Energiebedarf für die Klimasimulationen unserer Nutzerinnen und Nutzer drastisch reduzieren. Für ein Rechenzentrum, dessen Aufgabe die Unterstützung bei der Erforschung des Klimas ist, ist das kein zusätzlicher Vorteil – es ist Teil unseres Auftrags“, sagte Dr. Hendryk Bockelmann, Abteilungsleiter Anwendungen am DKRZ.
„Wir sind stolz darauf, unsere langjährige Zusammenarbeit mit dem DKRZ, einem der führenden Klimarechenzentren Europas, fortzusetzen. HLRE-5 baut auf jahrelanger gemeinsamer Innovationsarbeit im Bereich des energieeffizienten Supercomputings auf und zeigt, wie moderne digitale Infrastruktur exzellente Klimaforschung unterstützen kann“, ergänzte Dr. Martin Matzke, Head of Northern and Central Europe bei Bull.
HLRE-5 besteht aus zwei Partitionen: einer GPU-Partition, die auf Superchips des Typs NVIDIA GB200 Grace Blackwell basiert und den Großteil der Simulations- und KI-Leistung des Systems bereitstellt, sowie einer CPU-Partition auf Basis von NVIDIA Vera-CPUs. Diese bringt erstmals die ARM-Architektur in das Kernsystem des DKRZ und verbessert die Energieeffizienz für Rechenaufgaben, die nicht auf GPUs ausgeführt werden, erheblich. Alle Rechnerknoten sind über NVIDIA Quantum-2-InfiniBand vernetzt. Diese Netzwerktechnologie ermöglicht die Kommunikation zwischen den Knoten mit geringer Latenz und hoher Datenrate (400 GBit/s), auf die globale Klimamodelle mit einer Auflösung im Kilometerbereich angewiesen sind.
„Wir sind NVIDIA für die langjährige Unterstützung bei der Optimierung von ICON für GPUs dankbar, die auch dazu beigetragen hat, dass wir 2025 den ACM Gordon Bell Prize for Climate Modelling gewonnen haben. Wir freuen uns darauf, diese Zusammenarbeit auf HLRE-5 fortzusetzen“, betonte Dr. Jan Frederik Engels, Mitglied des Gordon-Bell-Teams und Systemdesigner für den HPC-Teil des HLRE-5.
Beim Datenspeicher geht eine neue Strategie über die Kapazität als primären Maßstab für die Dimensionierung hinaus und konzentriert sich stattdessen auf die effiziente Nutzung von Ressourcen durch intelligente Datenplatzierung und die Verteilung auf unterschiedliche Speicherhierarchien. Im Mittelpunkt steht die neue IBM Storage-Scale-System-6000, das 60 Petabytes Festplattenspeicher mit einem Datendurchsatz von bis zu 340 Gigabytes/s mit einem dedizierten Flash-Speicher mit 500 Terabytes kombiniert. In enger Zusammenarbeit mit IBM können fortschrittliche Funktionen zur bedarfsgesteuerten Verteilung der Daten auf die Speicherhierarchien sowie die Nutzung der Speicherressourcen für unterschiedliche Forschungsaufgaben analysiert und weiter optimiert werden.
Der Flash-Speicher adressiert die rasant wachsenden Anforderungen der KI und ist dafür konzipiert, die für anspruchsvolle KI-Anwendungen erforderliche Leistung bereitzustellen. Zusammen mit der Größe und Effizienz der kapazitätsorientierten Speicherhierarchien bietet sie der Forschungsgemeinschaft eine leistungsstarke Grundlage sowohl für HPC als auch für die nächste Generation KI-gestützter Forschung.
Wie bei den Vorgängergenerationen setzt das DKRZ zur Kühlung des Systems auf die patentierte Direct-Liquid-Cooling-Technologien (DLC) von Bull. Dabei fließt warmes Wasser in einem geschlossenen Kreislauf durch die Rechnerknoten und führt die Wärme wesentlich effizienter ab als eine Luftkühlung.
Seit mehreren Jahren liefert das DKRZ einen Teil dieser Wärme an den benachbarten Fachbereich Chemie der Universität Hamburg. Mit der Installation von HLRE-5 wird die Kühlinfrastruktur modernisiert, sodass ein größerer Anteil der Abwärme zur weiteren Nutzung zur Verfügung steht. Die Universität Hamburg plant, diese Nutzung auf weitere Gebäude auf und rund um den KlimaCampus auszuweiten.
Die Gesamtinvestition in das System beträgt 40 Millionen Euro und umfasst einen fünfjährigen Supportvertrag. Die Finanzierung erfolgt hauptsächlich durch die Helmholtz-Gemeinschaft, die Max-Planck-Gesellschaft und die Stadt Hamburg im Rahmen der langfristigen Finanzierungsvereinbarung für die HPC-Systeme am DKRZ. Dank zusätzlicher Mittel der Max-Planck-Gesellschaft und des Bundesministeriums für Forschung, Technologie und Raumfahrt im Rahmen der Hightech Agenda Deutschland (HTAD) konnte das System nochmals deutlich vergrößert werden.

content:
Architecture Winter Talks 2026: ORDER & AMBIGUITY

Plakat der Winter Talks 2026
| Copyright:
Download
Die internationale Vortragsreihe "Winter Talks" des Fachbereichs Architektur der Hochschule Bochum lädt in diesem Semester dazu ein, Ordnung und Mehrdeutigkeit in der Architektur neu zu betrachten.
Ordnung und Mehrdeutigkeit lassen sich als komplementäre Bedingungen begreifen, die es der Architektur ermöglichen, zugleich lesbar und offen zu bleiben. Im Zentrum der Vortragsreihe steht die Frage, wie architektonische Ordnung durch Struktur, Geometrie und Bewegung, Lesbarkeit und Stabilität erzeugen kann – und zugleich wie Mehrdeutigkeit durch komplexe Gestaltung Räume für verschiedene Nutzungen und Interpretationen öffnet. Die diesjährige Vortragsreihe versteht Architektur als einen Zustand, in dem eine geordnete Struktur Raum für Ungewissheit, Wandel und Pluralität bietet.
Die Veranstaltungen finden in englischer Sprache statt.
Beginn jeweils donnerstags, 18:00 Uhr
Blue Box Auditorium, Am Hochschulcampus 1, D-44801 Bochum
Kuratiert von @professurkinzelbach, ENBK Entwerfen und Baukonstruktion
Unterstützt durch: BDA Bochum
05.11.2026: OFFICE Kersten Geers David Van Severen, Brüssel
David Van Severen: Massstab und Perspektive
OFFICE ist ein in Brüssel ansässiges Architekturbüro, das 2002 von Kersten Geers und David Van Severen gegründet wurde. Es dient als Plattform, um Architektur im Kontext der zeitgenössischen Kultur und des urbanen Umfelds zu erforschen und entwickeln. Die Projekte, unterschiedlich in Maßstab und Typologie, sind zugleich pragmatisch und innovativ; sie sind tief in verschiedenen architektonischen Traditionen verwurzelt und schaffen einen Rahmen, in dem sich das Leben in all seiner Komplexität entfalten kann. Die internationale Tätigkeit des Büros, die unter anderem mit dem Silbernen Löwen und dem Aga Khan Award for Architecture gewürdigt wurde, geht einher mit Forschungsarbeit, Publikationen und Lehrtätigkeiten.
19.11.2026: MADE arhitekti, Riga
Miķelis Putrāms: Struktur und Flexibilität
Das Schaffen von Architektur ist ein komplexer Prozess, der sowohl Struktur als auch Flexibilität erfordert. Das Büro MADE arhitekti unter der Leitung der Partner Linda Krūmiņa und Miķelis Putrāms hat Projekte für private Bauherren sowie öffentliche Aufträge mit Präzision und Engagement umgesetzt. Gebäude bringen einen gestalterischen Ansatz zum Ausdruck – doch noch wichtiger ist, dass sie unser Verhalten prägen. Flexibilität wird somit zu einem wirkungsvollen Instrument, um sowohl das Gebäude selbst als auch den Prozess seiner Entstehung zu steuern.
26.11.2026: ADEPT, Copenhagen
Simon Lyager Poulsen: Was wir nicht wissen, dass wir es nicht wissen
Indem sie soziale und urbane Synergien fördern, zeichnen sich die Entwürfe von ADEPT als „anti-ikonische“ Typologien aus – konzipiert als Rahmen für das Leben, fest verankert im jeweiligen Kontext, am menschlichen Maßstab orientiert und auf einen verantwortungsvollen Umgang mit Ressourcen ausgerichtet. Anstatt für eine festgelegte Zukunft zu planen, nähert sich das Büro seinen Entwürfen über Szenarien und offene Fragestellungen; dabei werden architektonische Ideen mit der Fähigkeit zur Anpassung, Aneignung und Veränderung in Einklang gebracht. Auf diese Weise schafft das Büro Gebäude und Orte, die nicht nur das aufnehmen können, was wir bereits kennen, sondern auch das, was wir heute noch nicht vorhersehen können.

title: Giga Storage secures financing, grid connection for 1.4 GWh CATL BESS project in Germany - Energy Storage
content: Giga Storage has closed financing for its large-scale “Albatross” battery energy storage system near Neuenkirchen in Lower Saxony, Germany. A consortium of seven banks is providing the Dutch developer with €260 million ($281 million) in debt capital for the project. Construction is scheduled to begin in early 2027, while commissioning is planned for early 2029. The project will have a power output of 350 MW and capacity of 1.4 GWh, with a four-hour duration. The grid connection agreement with Amprion has also been signed. Commissioning is now scheduled for early 2029. The participating lenders in the financing round are ABN Amro, Hamburg Commercial Bank, ING, Rabobank, Siemens Financial Services via Siemens Bank, SMBC, and Société Générale. Giga Storage had previously announced in early October that the project had reached ready-to-build status. At that time, the company still expected the final investment decision in the fourth quarter, and commissioning was originally slated for 2028. Meanwhile, Giga Storage also signed a grid connection agreement with German transmission system operator (TSO) Amprion, and the agreement was concluded on October 14. Amprion stated that this marks the company’s first grid connection contract for a large-scale battery storage facility. The system will be connected directly to the 380 kV transmission grid at the Merzen substation. The storage facility will consist of 264 battery containers, 96 medium-voltage transformers, and two high-voltage transformers. According to Giga Storage, CATL will handle the engineering, construction, and maintenance of the facility, working alongside several European subcontractors. “Albatross” is Giga Storage’s first utility-scale storage project in Germany. Together with its “Leopard” project in the Netherlands and the “Green Turtle” project in Belgium, the company states that it currently has storage projects with a combined output of around 1.4 GW and a total capacity of 5.6 GWh under construction. title: Trina Storage to supply 196 MWh battery system for Japan's Nozu project - Energy Storage
content: Trina Storage, the battery energy storage business of China’s Trinasolar, has been selected to supply battery storage systems for the 50 MW/196 MWh AEJ Nozu project in Oita Prefecture, Japan. The company announced the contract on October 14, with project completion scheduled for the third quarter of 2028. Located in Nishihata, Nozu Town, Usuki City, the grid-scale facility will have a nominal storage duration of approximately 3.9 hours. It is being developed by Nozomi Energy, a Japanese renewable energy platform backed by infrastructure investor Actis, through its project company AEJ Nozu Storage Power Plant Contract Company. The project secured a capacity contract in Japan’s fiscal 2023 Long-Term Decarbonization Auction, providing inflation-linked capacity payments over 20 years. Nozomi Energy reached financial close in September 2026 after securing non-recourse project financing from Japan’s Aozora Bank. The financing amount has not been disclosed. China Energy Engineering Shanxi Electric Power Engineering Co., Ltd. has separately secured the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the project’s balance-of-plant works. The company said the development had obtained key land and grid-connection permits. Trina Storage will supply its Elementa 2 Pro battery energy storage solution, built around standardized 5 MWh containerized units. According to the manufacturer’s technical documentation, the system uses its proprietary 314 Ah lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, with a nominal energy capacity of 5.015 MWh per container and a DC voltage architecture approaching 1,500 V. The system is housed in a standard 20-foot high-cube container and incorporates liquid cooling, battery monitoring and multiple layers of safety protection. Trina Storage says its thermal management design maintains cell temperature differences within 2.5 C, while the system features IP67-rated battery modules and an IP55-rated enclosure. Additional safety features include temperature and smoke monitoring, active ventilation and fire suppression systems. Trina Storage specifies a cell cycle life of up to 12,000 cycles for the product, although the company has not disclosed project-specific operating assumptions or performance guarantees for the Nozu installation. The manufacturer said its Japanese operations will support system configuration, technical consultation, delivery coordination and after-sales services, working with local project partners to address technical and regulatory requirements. “For Nozu and other projects in Japan, our focus is on combining advanced technology with strong local capabilities,” said Leo Zhao, head of energy storage for Asia-Pacific at Trina Storage. The contract adds to Trina Storage’s Japanese project portfolio, which includes a separate 160 MWh utility-scale BESS in the Kyushu region. In September, the company also signed a memorandum of understanding with Japanese developer AMP-lify covering approximately 1 GWh of potential grid-connected storage projects using its newer Elementa 3 series. Nozu is among the battery storage developments supported by Japan’s long-term decarbonization capacity mechanism, which is intended to encourage investment in low-carbon generation and flexible power resources. The project’s long-term contracted capacity revenue provides greater revenue visibility for its developer, while construction, equipment delivery and commissioning remain ahead of its planned 2028 completion. The value of Trina Storage’s supply contract and the project’s total investment cost have not been disclosed. title: Samsung SDI signs 1 GWh supply agreement for US-made NCA battery storage - Energy Storage
content: Samsung SDI has signed a deal to supply 1 GWh of nickel cobalt aluminum (NCA) battery storage to a single US customer, with all cells and modules to be manufactured in the United States. Under the agreement with utility and independent power producer Alpha Omega Power (APO), Samsung SDI is expected to deliver its Samsung Battery Box (SBB) 1.7 containerized energy storage to projects scheduled to being construction in 2027. These will include projects in the Western Electricity Coordinating Council (WECC) and Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) energy markets. All cells and modules for the  battery containers covered in the supply agreement will be manufactured at Samsung SDI’s StarPlus Energy (SPE) plant in Kokomo, Indiana, according to the manufacturer, with delivery expected before the end of 2026. In choosing Samsung SDI as a supplier, APO is putting significant investment into NCA chemistry battery storage in a global market where cells using lithium iron phosphate (LFP) based chemistry continue to lead. The investment also comes as the US government mulls further restrictions on imported power equipment. Samsung SDI reports that the SBB 1.7 uses a high-nickel NCA chemistry and delivers 17% higher energy density than its predecessor, the SBB 1.5, while maintaining the same 20-foot footprint. The manufacturer also highlights fire safety as a key feature of the design, noting the battery storage solution incorporates Samsung SDI’s proprietary Enhanced Direct Injection technology, which directly injects fire-extinguishing agents into individual battery modules. The latest agreement means Samsung SDI has been contracted to supply a total of 1.5 GWh of energy storage to APO, following an earlier supply contract signed in 2025. In a press release, Fabrice Hudry president ESS of Samsung SDI America, said the company’s “differentiated technology” and US production capabilities will see it continue to expand in the North American ESS market. Paul Choi, CEO of Alpha Omega Power, added: “American-made ESS from Samsung SDI will play an important role in AOP’s continued growth. This second agreement strengthens our domestic supply chain supporting the next generation of energy infrastructure.” The post Samsung SDI signs 1 GWh supply agreement for US-made NCA battery storage appeared first on Energy Storage .
